items.prompt: Where were the friends flying to?
items.passage:
Last March, my friend Dilnoza and I planned a short holiday in Istanbul. Our flight from Tashkent was supposed to leave at 6:40 in the morning, so we agreed to meet at the airport at four o'clock. I had set two alarms, but when I woke up, my phone had died during the night because I had forgotten to charge it. By the time I realised what had happened, it was already ten past four.

I jumped into a taxi and begged the driver to hurry. The traffic was light, and we reached the airport in twenty-five minutes. Dilnoza was waiting at the entrance with a worried face. She told me that the check-in desk had closed five minutes earlier, because the airline wanted passengers to arrive at least ninety minutes before departure. We ran to the desk anyway, but the clerk said that nothing could be done and that our seats had already been given to people on the waiting list.

At first we were very upset. If I had charged my phone, we would have caught the plane without any trouble. However, Dilnoza reminded me that complaining would not solve anything. We went to the information office, where a kind woman named Malika explained our options. We could change our tickets for a small fee, and the next flight to Istanbul would leave at half past two in the afternoon. The fee was forty dollars each, which seemed fair compared with buying completely new tickets.

We paid the fee and then had eight hours to wait. Instead of sitting in the terminal, we took a bus into the city and had a long breakfast in a small cafe near the old bazaar. We ate fresh bread, drank tea, and laughed about the whole situation. Later we walked through a park and sent photos to our families, who had been told that our trip would begin a little late.

The afternoon flight was comfortable, and we landed in Istanbul at about six in the evening. Our hotel had kept our room, although the receptionist said that most hotels would not have waited for us so long. We were lucky. Since that day, I always charge my phone before going to bed and I buy an old-fashioned alarm clock for every important journey. Dilnoza says that I should also learn to arrive early, and I have to admit that she is right.

items.prompt: Where did the narrator travel with his cousin?
items.passage:
Traveling by night train has always been one of my favourite ways to see Uzbekistan. Last autumn, I took the evening train from Tashkent to Khiva with my cousin Bobur. The journey was scheduled to take about nineteen hours, which seemed long, but we had been told that the sleeping cars were comfortable and cheap. We boarded at seven in the evening and found our compartment, which had four beds, a small table, and a window with a thick curtain.

Two other passengers shared the compartment with us. One was an elderly teacher called Gulsara, who was going to visit her grandchildren, and the other was a young engineer named Timur, who worked in the desert near Navoi. As soon as the train left the station, Gulsara opened a large bag and offered us samsa, apples and sweet tea from her thermos. She said that it was impossible to travel in Uzbekistan without sharing food, and nobody argued with her.

After dinner, Timur told us that the train had been built in the 1980s and that it had been repaired several times. Perhaps that was why it moved so slowly at night. The beds were narrow, and the rocking motion made it difficult to fall asleep at first. Still, around midnight I finally closed my eyes, and I did not wake up until a conductor knocked on the door at six o'clock and asked whether we wanted breakfast.

The morning view was amazing. Outside the window, there was nothing but yellow sand, a few camels, and a thin line of power poles that stretched towards the horizon. Bobur took dozens of photographs, though he complained that the glass was dirty. At around nine, the train stopped at a small station for twenty minutes, and we bought hot bread and cold water from a woman who was selling them on the platform.

We arrived in Khiva at two in the afternoon, almost an hour late. Although we were tired, we felt that we had really crossed the country, not simply flown over it. If you ever have the chance, take the night train at least once. You will meet people, eat good food, and see a part of the country that most tourists never notice.

items.prompt: How much did one night cost?
items.passage:
I stayed at the Blue Door Hostel in Lisbon for six nights in June, and I want to share an honest review for other travellers. I found it online after reading that it was close to the old town and cost only eighteen euros a night. I booked a bed in a dormitory for eight people, which is usually the cheapest option. When I arrived, the receptionist, a cheerful man named Tiago, gave me a locker key and a map and explained everything slowly, because my Portuguese was non-existent.

The location is excellent. It takes only ten minutes to walk to the famous yellow tram stop, and the nearest supermarket is just around the corner. The building itself is old, and some of the stairs are quite steep, so it is not ideal for anyone with heavy luggage. My room was on the third floor, and I had to carry my suitcase up without any elevator. Next time, I will definitely pack lighter.

The dormitory was clean, and every bed had a curtain, a reading lamp and a power socket. However, the air conditioning was broken during my first two nights, and it was extremely hot. I told Tiago about the problem, and he apologised and promised that a technician would come the next morning. It was fixed on the second day, as he had said, and the owner even offered me a free breakfast to make up for it.

One of the best things about the hostel is the social atmosphere. Every evening at eight, the staff organise a free dinner on the roof terrace, where guests can eat pasta, salad and fruit together. I met travellers from Brazil, Japan and Poland, and one night we all went to a small restaurant to listen to live music. The kitchen is also available for guests, although it can get crowded around seven.

In conclusion, I would give the Blue Door Hostel four stars out of five. The staff are friendly, the price is fair, and the location is great. It would get five stars if the stairs were easier and the air conditioning had worked from the beginning. I would happily stay there again, and I recommend it to anyone who wants to meet people while travelling on a budget.

items.prompt: Who drove the car?
items.passage:
Day one. We left Samarkand at nine in the morning in my uncle's old blue car. There were four of us: me, my sister Nilufar, my friend Aziz and my uncle Rustam, who insisted on driving because he said nobody else knew the mountain roads. Our plan was to cross the Fergana Valley in five days and visit three small towns where my uncle had lived as a young man. We packed bread, boiled eggs, tea and a battery radio, which turned out to be very useful.

Day two. The road climbed steadily through the mountains, and by noon the temperature had dropped noticeably. We stopped at a roadside stall where an old man sold dried apricots and walnuts. Rustam spoke with him for almost half an hour, and it turned out that they had studied at the same school forty years earlier. The man gave us a bag of apricots for free, and we promised to visit him on the way back.

Day three. Disaster nearly struck. About two hours after breakfast, the car began to make a strange noise, and then white smoke came from the engine. Rustam pulled over and told us not to worry. If we had not been so close to a village, we would have been in serious trouble. A mechanic named Sherzod looked at the engine, replaced a small broken pipe and refused to take any money. He only asked us to send him a postcard from Fergana.

Day four. We reached the first town in the afternoon. Rustam showed us the house where he used to live, which is now a small bakery. The owner, a smiling woman, let us inside and served us hot bread straight from the oven. Nilufar said it was the best bread she had ever tasted, and I agreed. That evening we slept in a tiny guesthouse, and the owner told us stories about the valley until midnight.

Day five. On our last day, we drove slowly and stopped often to take photographs. By the time we arrived at the final town, all of us were tired but happy. If I could repeat the journey, I would not change anything, except perhaps checking the car before we left. Rustam laughs whenever I say this and promises that his car will never break down again.

items.prompt: Where was Sardor going to fly after Frankfurt?
items.passage:
When Sardor landed in Frankfurt on a rainy Tuesday afternoon, he expected a quiet connection to Toronto. He had travelled for nearly ten hours, and all he wanted was a hot meal and a short sleep. However, when he reached the luggage belt, he waited for forty minutes while every other passenger collected a bag and left. Finally the belt stopped, and he realised that his large blue suitcase had not arrived.

He walked to the lost luggage office, where a tired employee gave him a form to fill in. He had to describe the suitcase, list what was inside and write the address of his hotel. Sardor explained that he was flying to Canada later the same evening, so the bag had to be found quickly. The employee told him that the suitcase had probably been sent to another airport by mistake, and that the airline would try to find it within twenty-four hours.

Sardor was worried because his suitcase contained his laptop charger, two business suits and important documents for a meeting. He had been told by his manager that the meeting was the most important event of the year. The employee suggested that he should buy some basic clothes and keep the receipts, because the airline would pay back up to one hundred and fifty euros. That calmed him down a little.

In the airport shops, he bought a clean shirt, a toothbrush and a small bag. Then he called his manager and explained the problem. His manager, Ms Karimova, was understanding and said that the meeting could be moved by one day if necessary. Sardor thanked her and decided to continue his journey, leaving his address in Toronto with the airline staff.

Two days later, a courier knocked on the door of his hotel with a large blue suitcase. It had travelled to Madrid before coming back to Frankfurt and then to Canada. Everything was inside, though the laptop charger was slightly bent. Since then, Sardor always puts one change of clothes and his documents in his hand luggage, and he advises everyone to do the same.

items.prompt: How much was the day ticket?
items.passage:
My first morning in Prague began with a decision. I had only two days in the city, and I wanted to see as much as possible without spending too much money. At the hotel, the receptionist recommended the hop-on hop-off bus, which cost twenty-two euros for a day ticket. She said that the buses ran every twenty minutes between nine in the morning and five in the afternoon and that headphones were included in the price.

I bought my ticket at the stop near the Astronomical Clock and took a seat on the open top deck. The weather was cool but sunny, and I was glad that I had brought a jacket. The audio guide was available in twelve languages, and I chose English. It explained that the city had been founded more than a thousand years ago and that many of its buildings had survived the wars without serious damage.

The route passed the Charles Bridge, the National Theatre and the huge castle that stands above the river. I got off at the castle stop and spent two hours inside, where I saw the cathedral and a small street called the Golden Lane. According to the guide, goldsmiths had once lived there, although later the houses were rented by writers. One of them was Franz Kafka, who stayed in a tiny blue house for a few months.

For lunch, I went to a traditional restaurant and tried goulash with bread dumplings. The portion was so big that I could not finish it, and the waiter laughed and said that all foreigners made the same mistake. Afterwards I returned to the bus and continued towards the Jewish Quarter, where I visited an old synagogue and a cemetery with thousands of crooked stones.

In the evening, I was exhausted but delighted. The bus tour had given me a clear map of the city in my head, and the next day I returned on foot to the places I liked best. If you are planning a short visit, I would strongly recommend this kind of tour. It is not the cheapest way to travel, but it saves time and gives you a general picture before you explore on your own.

items.prompt: Where did the writer begin the journey?
items.passage:
Before I left for Vietnam, my mother worried about everything: the food, the heat and the traffic. I promised to send her a message every evening, and I kept my promise for the first two weeks. I started my journey in Hanoi, where I stayed in the Old Quarter. The streets were full of motorbikes, and crossing the road felt like a game. A local woman told me to walk slowly and steadily, and never to run, because the drivers would simply go around me.

From Hanoi, I took a night bus to Hue, a journey of about thirteen hours. The seats could be lowered into beds, but they were made for people shorter than me, and I hardly slept. In Hue, I visited the imperial city, which had been badly damaged during the war and was slowly being repaired. A guide called Linh showed me the gardens and told me that the emperors had lived there until the middle of the twentieth century.

The highlight of my trip was Hoi An, a small town famous for its tailors and lanterns. On my second day, I ordered a linen shirt, and the tailor measured me and promised that it would be ready by the evening. It really was, and it fitted perfectly. I paid only twenty dollars, which was much less than I would have paid at home. In the evening, the whole town was lit by hundreds of coloured lanterns, and I sat by the river with a cold coconut drink.

The food was the best part of the journey. I tried noodle soup for breakfast, grilled pork with rice for lunch and fresh spring rolls for dinner. At first, I was afraid of street food, but a Canadian traveller named Mark taught me to choose stalls that were full of locals. I followed his advice and never got sick.

After three weeks, I flew home with a light heart and a heavy bag. My mother met me at the airport and cried, then laughed, then asked what I wanted to eat. I told her noodle soup, and she looked at me as if I had gone mad. If I could go back, I would stay another month, and this time I would bring her with me.

items.prompt: Where did the family start the journey?
items.passage:
Every summer, my family travels to the island of Hvar by ferry, and every summer something unexpected happens. This year, we left our home in Zagreb on a Friday morning and drove to the port of Split, which took about four hours. My father had booked tickets in advance, because in July the ferries are usually full, and people who arrive without a reservation can wait for hours. We had a space for the car and four seats on the upper deck.

The ferry was supposed to depart at one o'clock, but it was delayed by almost forty minutes because of a strong wind. While we waited, my little brother Luka ate two ice creams, and my mother read the newspaper. A friendly sailor explained that the captain would not leave the port until the sea was calm enough. He said that safety was more important than time, and nobody complained.

When the ferry finally moved, everyone went to the deck to watch the harbour disappear. The water was a deep, bright blue, and white birds followed the ship the whole way. After about an hour, a group of dolphins appeared beside the boat, jumping in and out of the water. Luka was so excited that he almost fell over the railing, and my father had to hold him by the shirt.

We arrived in Hvar at half past three. The town was crowded with tourists, but our apartment was in a quiet village on the other side of the island. My aunt, who has lived there for twenty years, was waiting for us with a big smile and a basket of fresh figs. That evening we ate fish at a small restaurant by the sea, and the sunset turned the whole sky orange.

Looking back, the delay did not matter at all. In fact, if the ferry had left on time, we might have missed the dolphins. My father says that this is the lesson of every journey: the best moments are the ones that nobody has planned. I think he is probably right, although I still prefer to arrive on time.

items.prompt: Where did the couple start their holiday?
items.passage:
Last summer, my husband and I decided to try something completely different: a cycling holiday in the Netherlands. We had both cycled to work for years, but never more than ten kilometres in one day. Our friends said we were crazy, and my sister laughed when we told her that our route was almost two hundred kilometres long. Still, we booked a company that would carry our luggage from hotel to hotel, so we only had to worry about our legs.

We began in Amsterdam on a warm Monday morning. The guide, a cheerful woman called Anouk, gave us two bicycles, a map and a small repair kit. She told us that the Dutch cycling paths were the best in the world and that cyclists always had priority over cars. She was right. Even in the busy city centre, there were separate lanes, traffic lights for bikes and enormous parking places full of bicycles.

On the second day, we left the city and rode through fields of tulips, which were slightly past their best but still colourful. The land was perfectly flat, and the wind was our only problem. When it blew against us, we moved very slowly and had to stop every half an hour for a drink. At lunch, we bought cheese, bread and apples from a farm shop, and the farmer let us sit in his garden to eat them.

The third day was the hardest. It rained from morning to evening, and our clothes became so wet that we could not stop laughing. We reached a tiny village called Edam, where our hotel had been built three hundred years ago. The owner gave us dry towels and hot soup, and I have never been so grateful for a bowl of soup in my life.

By the end of the week, we had covered one hundred and eighty-five kilometres. Our legs hurt, but we felt proud and healthy. My husband has already suggested that next year we should cycle in Denmark. I told him that I would think about it, but I would need a much softer saddle.

items.prompt: How many visitors came to Bukhara last year?
items.answer: About four hundred and twenty thousand
items.passage:
The Tourist Information Office in the town of Bukhara has published its annual report for the previous year, and the results are encouraging. According to the report, the town welcomed about four hundred and twenty thousand visitors, which is eighteen percent more than the year before. Of these, nearly half came from abroad, mainly from Germany, France, South Korea and Russia. The director of the office, Mr Akmal Yusupov, said that he was delighted but not surprised, because the government had improved the airport and opened a new fast train line.

The report also describes the changes that visitors have noticed. Many historic buildings were cleaned and repaired during the year, including a small madrasa near the old market that had been closed for almost a decade. New signs in five languages were placed along the main streets, and a free mobile application was created to help tourists find restaurants, shops and toilets. Mr Yusupov explained that earlier many guests had complained about getting lost in the narrow lanes of the old quarter.

One of the most successful projects was a new walking tour called Stories of the Silk Road. The tour was led by students from the local university, who had been trained by experienced guides during the winter. It lasted two hours and cost only five dollars, and more than eleven thousand people joined it. The office received hundreds of positive comments, and many guests said that they enjoyed hearing real stories rather than long lists of dates.

Not everything was perfect, however. The report admits that the town still has too few hotels in the middle price range. In the busiest months, visitors had to book rooms two or three months in advance, and some of them stayed in neighbouring towns instead. Another problem was the rubbish left in the streets after large festivals. The office plans to place more bins and to employ ten extra cleaners next spring.

Looking forward, the director hopes to reach half a million visitors within three years. To achieve this, the office will open a small museum of local crafts and organise a monthly food market. He also wants to encourage tourists to stay longer. At present, the average visitor stays only two nights, but he believes that four nights would be much better for local businesses.

The Tourist Information Office in the town of Bukhara has published its annual report for the previous year, and the results are encouraging. According to the report, the town welcomed about four hundred and twenty thousand visitors, which is eighteen percent more than the year before. Of these, nearly half came from abroad, mainly from Germany, France, South Korea and Russia. The director of the office, Mr Akmal Yusupov, said that he was delighted but not surprised, because the government had improved the airport and opened a new fast train line.

The report also describes the changes that visitors have noticed. Many historic buildings were cleaned and repaired during the year, including a small madrasa near the old market that had been closed for almost a decade. New signs in five languages were placed along the main streets, and a free mobile application was created to help tourists find restaurants, shops and toilets. Mr Yusupov explained that earlier many guests had complained about getting lost in the narrow lanes of the old quarter.

One of the most successful projects was a new walking tour called Stories of the Silk Road. The tour was led by students from the local university, who had been trained by experienced guides during the winter. It lasted two hours and cost only five dollars, and more than eleven thousand people joined it. The office received hundreds of positive comments, and many guests said that they enjoyed hearing real stories rather than long lists of dates.

Not everything was perfect, however. The report admits that the town still has too few hotels in the middle price range. In the busiest months, visitors had to book rooms two or three months in advance, and some of them stayed in neighbouring towns instead. Another problem was the rubbish left in the streets after large festivals. The office plans to place more bins and to employ ten extra cleaners next spring.

Looking forward, the director hopes to reach half a million visitors within three years. To achieve this, the office will open a small museum of local crafts and organise a monthly food market. He also wants to encourage tourists to stay longer. At present, the average visitor stays only two nights, but he believes that four nights would be much better for local businesses.

items.prompt: Why did the writer need to learn to drive?
items.answer: The bus to work ran only twice a day
items.passage:
When I moved to Scotland for my studies, I did not own a car, and I thought I would never need one. Then I found a part-time job at a farm shop twenty kilometres outside Edinburgh, and the only bus came twice a day. My boss, a patient man called Hamish, said that I should learn to drive, and he offered to lend me his old car for lessons. At home in Uzbekistan I had a licence, but driving on the left side of the road was a completely new challenge.

My first lesson took place on a quiet Sunday morning in an empty car park. Hamish sat beside me and repeated the same words many times: keep left, look right, stay calm. I turned on the windscreen wipers instead of the indicator at least five times, and he laughed every time. After an hour, I could drive in a straight line, though I still felt that everything was happening on the wrong side.

The real problems began on the roads. Roundabouts in Britain go clockwise, which means that I had to give way to traffic coming from the right, and I could never remember it. Once I stopped in the middle of a roundabout because I had become confused, and a driver behind me honked for a full minute. I was so embarrassed that I wanted to hide under the seat. Hamish simply said that every learner had done something similar.

After three weeks of practice, I felt confident enough to take a driving test. The examiner was a serious woman who spoke very little. She asked me to park between two cars, to turn around in a narrow street and to drive along a busy road for twenty minutes. At the end, she checked her papers and said that I had made only three small mistakes, which was within the limit. I had passed.

Today I drive to work every morning, and I enjoy it. Whenever I visit my family in Tashkent, I have to remind myself to switch sides. My father finds this hilarious, and he always sits beside me with his hand ready on the door, just in case.
options: The bus to work ran only twice a day
He wanted to buy a car

items.prompt: Where did the friends go camping?
items.passage:
Last July, six friends from my university decided to spend a long weekend camping in the Chimgan mountains, about eighty kilometres from Tashkent. I had never slept in a tent before, so I was both excited and nervous. Our leader, Jamshid, had been camping since he was a child, and he made a long list of everything we should bring. It included sleeping bags, warm sweaters, a gas cooker, torches and, in his words, a very large amount of food.

We left the city on Friday at noon in a rented minibus. The road to the mountains was winding, and Madina, who always feels sick in cars, had to sit in the front seat. After two hours, we arrived at a small village, where we left the bus and carried our bags for another hour along a narrow path. The air was fresh and cool, and the only sounds were birds and a river somewhere below us.

We chose a flat place beside a stream and began to build our tents. It turned out to be much harder than it had looked on the video that Jamshid had shown us. The wind kept taking the cloth, and Farrukh got tangled in the ropes and fell over twice. After forty minutes, all three tents were standing, and we celebrated with tea and sweet biscuits.

That night, we made a fire and cooked rice with vegetables. The sky was so clear that we could see thousands of stars, and Jamshid pointed out the constellations. Around eleven, it began to get cold, and I realised that I had forgotten my warm socks. Madina lent me a pair of hers, and I slept better than I had expected.

On Saturday morning, we climbed to a small lake, which took us three hours. The water was ice cold, but Farrukh insisted on swimming, and he came out shouting. On Sunday, we packed up, cleaned the area and took all our rubbish with us. Jamshid said that a good camper leaves nothing behind except footprints. I am now planning to buy my own tent for next summer.

items.prompt: Which country did the writer apply to study in?
items.passage:
Two years ago, I applied for a student visa to study in Germany, and the experience taught me more about patience than any book. My university in Tashkent had accepted me for a master's programme in engineering, and I was supposed to start in October. The embassy told me that I had to book an appointment online, but for the first three weeks every date was full. I checked the website every morning at seven, hoping that somebody had cancelled.

Finally, I found an appointment on the ninth of July. I spent a whole week preparing my documents. I needed my passport, an acceptance letter, a bank statement, health insurance, photographs and a certificate that proved my German level. My older brother Otabek, who had applied for a visa before, advised me to make two copies of everything and to arrange the papers in the order that the embassy had listed. It looked boring, but it saved me a lot of time later.

On the day of the interview, I arrived at the embassy two hours early because I was afraid of being late. There was already a long queue, and everyone looked nervous. After going through security, I waited for another hour in a small room. My heart was beating so fast that I could hardly read the form in my hands. At last, they called my number, and I went to a window where a young officer greeted me politely.

The interview lasted only seven minutes. The officer asked why I had chosen Germany, how I would pay for my living expenses and what I planned to do after graduation. I answered simply and honestly. He checked my documents carefully, asked me to sign a paper and told me that I would receive a decision within three weeks. I left the building feeling both relieved and uncertain.

The decision arrived in twelve days, and it was positive. I cried a little in the kitchen, and my mother made plov to celebrate. Looking back, the waiting was harder than the interview. If anyone asks me for advice today, I always say the same thing: start early, stay organised and be honest.

items.prompt: What is an Istanbulkart?
items.passage:
Many people think that visiting Istanbul requires taxis, but I discovered that the public transport system is cheap, fast and often more interesting. I spent a weekend there last April with my friend Kamila, and we decided not to use a single taxi. On Friday evening we landed at the airport and bought an Istanbulkart, a small plastic card that works on buses, trams, metros and ferries. We put twenty euros on it, which turned out to be enough for the entire trip.

Our hotel was in the district of Sultanahmet, and to get there, we took the metro and then a tram. The tram was crowded, but a young man stood up and offered Kamila his seat, which surprised us. He told us that in Istanbul, people are used to helping visitors. When we got off, he even walked with us for five minutes to show us the right street, because our map was confusing.

On Saturday morning, we took a ferry across the Bosphorus to the Asian side of the city. The ride lasted twenty minutes, and the price was less than a cup of coffee. On the deck, we bought hot tea in tiny glasses and fed bread to the seagulls, which followed the boat in a noisy cloud. The view of the mosques and the old palaces on the hills was something that I will never forget.

The only problem happened on Saturday night. We wanted to return to our hotel after dinner, but the tram had stopped running earlier than we expected. A friendly bus driver, who spoke a little English, explained that we had to take another route. We had to change buses twice, and the journey took almost an hour. Kamila was a bit annoyed, but I thought it was a good adventure.

On Sunday, we spent our last hours in the Grand Bazaar and returned to the airport by metro. Our card still had three euros left, and Kamila used it to buy a bottle of water. In total, we had spent less on transport in three days than I usually spend on a single taxi at home. I would recommend this way of travelling to anyone who is not afraid of crowds.

items.prompt: Where was Zarina studying?
items.passage:
It was the twenty-third of December, and Zarina was trying to get home for the holidays. She was studying in Moscow and had bought a train ticket to Tashkent weeks earlier, hoping to arrive on the twenty-fifth. However, a heavy snowstorm had hit the region, and when she reached the station at eight in the evening, the departure board showed that her train had been delayed by four hours. The waiting hall was packed with tired, worried passengers sitting on their luggage.

Zarina found a small space near the wall and took out her book. Beside her sat an older man named Viktor, who was travelling to Novosibirsk to see his daughter. He offered her a cup of hot tea from his flask and explained that he had been waiting for six hours. Trains were stopping everywhere because the snow had covered the rails, and the workers were clearing them as fast as they could. He said that he had experienced worse winters, but he did not look happy.

At midnight, an announcement said that the delay would be extended until five in the morning. Many people groaned, and a few began to argue with the station staff. Zarina decided to stay calm. She called her mother and explained the situation, and her mother told her not to panic and promised that the family would wait for her no matter how late she was. That conversation made her feel much better.

The train finally left at half past five. Inside, the carriages were warm, and the conductor gave every passenger a free blanket and a hot drink to apologise for the trouble. Zarina fell asleep almost immediately and woke up after noon, when the train was passing through snowy forests. She spent the rest of the journey chatting with other travellers and playing cards.

She arrived in Tashkent on the morning of the twenty-seventh, two days later than planned. Her family was standing on the platform with flowers and a huge pot of soup. Although she had missed the holiday dinner, her mother said that they would simply celebrate again. Zarina smiled and thought that this was the warmest welcome of her life.

The waiting hall was packed with tired, worried passengers sitting on their luggage.

Zarina found a small space near the wall and took out her book. Beside her sat an older man named Viktor, who was travelling to Novosibirsk to see his daughter. He offered her a cup of hot tea from his flask and explained that he had been waiting for six hours. Trains were stopping everywhere because the snow had covered the rails, and the workers were clearing them as fast as they could. He said that he had experienced worse winters, but he did not look happy.

At midnight, an announcement said that the delay would be extended until five in the morning. Many people groaned, and a few began to argue with the station staff. Zarina decided to stay calm. items.prompt: How long had Dilnoza been looking for a job?
items.passage:
Dilnoza had been looking for a job for almost four months when she received an email from a travel company in Samarkand. The company wanted to invite her for an interview on Thursday at ten o'clock. She had studied tourism at university, but she had never worked in an office before, so she felt both excited and nervous.

The night before the interview, Dilnoza prepared carefully. She read everything she could find about the company, which had been founded in 2009 and organised tours for visitors from Europe and Asia. She also wrote a list of questions she expected to hear, such as "Why do you want this job?" and "What is your biggest weakness?". Her older brother Rustam, who works as an engineer, listened to her answers and told her to speak more slowly. "If you rush, people will think you are afraid," he said.

On Thursday morning she left home at eight because she did not want to be late. The bus was crowded, and it arrived at the office twenty minutes early. She waited in a small room with a glass of water and tried to breathe calmly. At ten exactly, a tall woman called Mrs. Karimova invited her in. Another manager, Mr. Brown, from England, was sitting next to her.

The interview lasted forty minutes. First, they asked about her education and her English. Dilnoza explained that she had lived in Tashkent for a year as an exchange student and that she had often helped foreign tourists at a local museum. Then Mr. Brown asked what she would do if a group of guests lost their luggage at the airport. Dilnoza thought for a moment and said she would stay calm, call the airline immediately, and arrange clean clothes for the guests until the bags were found. Both managers smiled at this answer.

The last question surprised her. Mrs. Karimova asked, "If you were offered the job, when could you start?" Dilnoza said she could begin in two weeks, because she had to finish a small course first. The managers said they would make a decision by Monday and thanked her for coming.

She left the building feeling lighter than she had expected. On Saturday, before the deadline, her phone rang. It was Mrs. Karimova, who told her that the company had chosen her from eleven candidates. The salary was not very high at the beginning, but there would be training and a chance to travel. Dilnoza accepted at once and called Rustam to thank him for his advice.

items.prompt: Where did Bobur work for his first real salary?
items.passage:
When I was nineteen, I got my first real salary. I had worked in my uncle's garage during the summers, but he only gave me a little pocket money. This time it was different. I had a proper job at a bookshop in Tashkent, and at the end of the month the manager handed me an envelope with two million som inside.

I remember walking home that evening and feeling very rich. In my head I had already spent the money three times. I wanted to buy a new phone, a pair of white sneakers, and a gift for my mother, who had supported me for years. My father, Akmal, was waiting on the balcony. When I showed him the envelope, he smiled and said, "Sit down, Bobur. Let's talk before you spend a single som."

He explained that money disappears quickly if you do not make a plan. He had learned this the hard way. When he received his first salary many years earlier, he had bought an expensive watch and then had to borrow money to pay for lunch for two weeks. He suggested that I divide my salary into three parts. Half would go to the things I needed, such as transport and food. One third would be for things I wanted. The rest, about two hundred thousand som, I should put into a savings account.

At first I thought this was boring. I wanted to enjoy the money immediately. But I agreed to try for one month. I bought the sneakers, which cost three hundred thousand som, and a scarf for my mother. The phone I postponed. Every evening I wrote down how much I had spent in a small notebook.

After a month I was surprised. For the first time, I still had money at the end of the month, and I did not feel poor at all. In fact, I felt proud. Two months later I had saved enough to buy the phone without borrowing anything. My mother cried a little when I gave her the scarf, and my father simply said, "If you had spent everything on the first day, you would still be waiting for that phone."

Today I work in a bank, and I often tell young colleagues the same thing: plan first, spend later. It is the best lesson my first salary taught me.

items.prompt: Why did Gulnora open the shop?
items.passage:
Gulnora Yusupova owns a small grocery shop near the bus station in Namangan. She opened it fifteen years ago, after she lost her job at a textile factory. At that time she had only three hundred dollars in savings, and many of her friends thought that opening a shop was a terrible idea. "You will never compete with the big supermarkets," they said. She decided to prove them wrong.

The first year was very difficult. She woke up at five every morning to buy fresh bread and vegetables from the wholesale market, and she did not close the shop until ten at night. She could not afford to hire anyone, so her husband and her teenage son helped her on weekends. Often she earned only enough to pay the rent and buy new goods for the next day. More than once she thought about giving up.

The turning point came when she noticed what customers really wanted. The big supermarkets were far away, and elderly people did not like walking so long. Gulnora started to deliver groceries for free to neighbours who could not leave their homes. She also allowed regular customers to buy on credit and pay at the end of the month. She wrote every name in a thick green notebook, and she never forgot who owed her money. Because she trusted people, people trusted her.

Slowly, the shop became popular. After four years she was able to rent the empty room next door and double the size of the shop. She added a small corner where customers could drink tea and read the newspaper. Many people said that this corner made her shop feel like a second home. Today she employs five workers, and her monthly sales are about ten times higher than in the first year.

When young people ask her for advice, Gulnora always gives the same three rules. First, know your customers by name. Second, never sell old products, even if you lose a little money. Third, keep learning. Last winter she attended a course on online marketing, and now she takes orders by phone and through a messaging app.

"Big shops have more goods," she says, "but small shops have more heart." Her customers clearly agree, because the shop is full every evening.

items.prompt: How long did Sanjar's journey to work take?
items.passage:
Two years ago, Sanjar worked in a big software company in the centre of Tashkent. Every morning he spent almost two hours on crowded buses and in traffic jams. By the time he reached his desk, he was already tired. When the company announced that employees could work from home three days a week, he was delighted.

At first, everything seemed perfect. He did not need to wake up at six, he could have breakfast with his wife, and he saved about two hundred thousand som a month on transport. However, after a few weeks he noticed some problems. His desk was in the living room, where his children played and his wife watched television. He found it hard to concentrate, and he often worked until late at night because the line between work and free time had disappeared.

He also missed his colleagues. In the office, he used to talk to them at lunch about football, films and new ideas. At home, he only saw them as small faces on a computer screen during meetings. One day he realised that he had not spoken to anyone outside his family for three days.

Sanjar decided to change his routine. First, he rented a small room near his flat, which he used as a quiet office. It cost him a hundred and fifty thousand som per month, but the result was worth it. Second, he set clear working hours, from nine to six, and he turned off his laptop at six sharp. Third, he arranged a weekly lunch with two friends from the company, so that he could keep in touch with real people.

The new routine worked well. His boss noticed that he finished projects faster, and last spring Sanjar was promoted to team leader. He now advises other employees who are struggling with remote work. His advice is simple: have a separate place for work, keep fixed hours, and do not forget to meet people face to face.

"Working from home is a great opportunity," he says, "but only if you manage it, and do not let it manage you." His company is now thinking of offering similar rooms to all its staff.

items.prompt: What is Madina's job?
items.passage:
Madina is twenty-six years old and works as a nurse in a hospital in Bukhara. For years she had a problem that many young people have: no matter how much she earned, she never had anything left at the end of the month. Her salary was not small, but she spent it on coffee, taxis, clothes and online orders. When her grandmother became ill last year and the family needed money for medicine, Madina realised that she had nothing to offer.

That experience changed her. She decided to take saving seriously and began by looking carefully at her bank statements. She was shocked to discover that she had spent almost five hundred thousand som on taxis in a single month, even though the hospital was only fifteen minutes from her flat by bus. She had also bought three jackets that she hardly wore.

Madina created a simple budget. She wrote down her fixed costs, such as rent, electricity and phone, which together came to about forty percent of her income. Then she decided to move ten percent of her salary into a separate account on the very day she was paid. If the money was not in her main account, she could not spend it. She also deleted two shopping apps from her phone, which made impulse buying much harder.

The first months were not easy. Her friends invited her to cafes and she often had to say no. Sometimes she felt lonely and wondered if saving was worth it. But she found cheaper ways to meet them, such as cooking dinner at home or walking in the park on Sundays. Gradually she began to enjoy these evenings more than expensive restaurants.

After ten months, Madina had saved enough to cover three months of living costs. She felt much calmer, because she knew that she could handle an emergency. This spring she even used part of her savings to take a professional course in intensive care, which will help her earn a higher salary.

"Saving is not about being mean," she explains. "It is about buying yourself freedom." She now teaches a small group of younger nurses how to make a budget, and she hopes that none of them will have to learn the lesson the hard way.

items.prompt: In which city does Azamat live?
items.passage:
Everyone in the neighbourhood agreed that Azamat made the best bread in Khiva. For years he had baked at home for his family and friends, and people often told him he should sell it. His wife, Feruza, was the first to take the idea seriously. "If you do not try now," she said, "you will regret it when you are old."

The problem was money. A small bakery needed an oven, tables, flour, and rent for a place on a busy street. Azamat calculated that he needed about forty million som. He had saved fifteen million, and his brother promised to lend him another ten. For the rest, he went to a bank and asked for a loan. The bank officer, a serious man with round glasses, asked to see a business plan. Azamat had never written one, so he asked a former teacher to help him.

The plan took three weeks to prepare. It included the cost of ingredients, the expected number of customers, and a list of competitors. Azamat discovered that there were only two other bakeries within two kilometres, and neither of them opened before eight. He decided to open at five-thirty so that workers could buy fresh bread on their way to the factory. This small difference, he believed, would bring him a lot of customers.

The bank approved the loan, and in March the bakery opened. On the first day Azamat prepared two hundred loaves, and by nine o'clock they were all sold. He was so happy that he almost forgot to eat. However, in the second month a problem appeared: the price of flour rose by twenty percent. He could not raise his prices too much without losing customers, so he started buying flour directly from a farmer, which saved him money.

Today the bakery employs four people and produces about six hundred loaves a day. Azamat has also added sweet pastries, which are especially popular with children. His next plan is to open a second branch near the university.

"The most important thing," he says, "is to start. A good idea is only a dream until you open the door and light the oven."

items.prompt: How long did Olim work as an accountant?
items.passage:
For fifteen years, Olim worked as an accountant in a construction company in Fergana. He was good at his job, and his boss trusted him completely. However, every Sunday evening he felt a heavy feeling in his stomach, because he knew that he would have to return to the same grey office the next morning. He had never really wanted to be an accountant. He had chosen the profession because his parents believed it was safe.

On his fortieth birthday, his daughter Laylo gave him a small gift: a book about cooking. Olim had always enjoyed cooking for the family, and when he opened the book, he suddenly asked himself, "If I could do anything, what would I choose?" The answer came immediately. He wanted to teach people how to cook.

He did not leave his job at once. That would have been foolish, because he had a mortgage and two children at school. Instead, he started a cooking class on Saturday mornings in a rented kitchen. At first only three students came, all of them his neighbours. But he put short videos of his lessons on the internet, and within a few months, there were twenty students, some of whom travelled from other cities.

For a year Olim did both jobs. He slept very little, and his wife worried about his health. Nevertheless, he did not complain, because for the first time in years he was looking forward to the weekend. When his income from the classes became almost equal to his salary, he finally decided to resign. His boss was surprised and a little sad, but he wished him luck.

The beginning was risky. In the first three months of full-time teaching, Olim earned less than he had earned as an accountant. Yet he did not regret his choice. He opened a small cooking school with two assistants, and today it has more than a hundred students every month.

"People told me that forty was too late to change," he says. "But if I had waited until sixty, I would have lost twenty more years of happiness." He still does his own accounts, which he says is the only useful thing he kept from his old career.

items.prompt: What was Kamola studying?
items.passage:
Kamola was twenty-two and still a student of design when she began to sell things on the internet. It started by accident. She had knitted a wool hat for herself, and a classmate asked where she had bought it. When Kamola said that she had made it, the classmate immediately offered to pay twenty thousand som for one just like it.

That evening Kamola took photographs of three hats and posted them on a social media page called "Warm Heads". She did not expect much, but by morning she had received seven messages. By the end of the week, she had sold fourteen hats and could not keep up with the orders. She spent every evening knitting until midnight, and she learned an important lesson: demand can be bigger than your ability to produce.

Kamola decided to take the business more seriously. She bought wool in larger quantities, which made each hat cheaper to produce. She also asked her grandmother, who was a skilled knitter, to join her. In return, Kamola gave her a third of the profit. Together they could make about thirty hats a week.

The next challenge was delivery. At the beginning, Kamola had taken parcels to the post office herself, and this wasted a lot of time. She found a courier company that collected the parcels from her door for a small fee. Some customers complained that the hats arrived late, so she began to write the exact delivery date in each message, and the complaints stopped.

Photographs also made a big difference. When she started to take pictures in daylight, near a window, sales increased by almost half. She also learned to write honest descriptions. If a hat was a little smaller than usual, she said so, because she preferred a returned order to an unhappy customer.

By the end of the year, Kamola had more than two thousand followers and a monthly income that was higher than her mother's salary. After graduation, she plans to expand her shop to scarves and gloves. "My teachers say design needs a client," she says with a laugh. "I found mine before I finished my degree."

items.prompt: In which department does Shirin work?
items.passage:
Shirin had been working in the marketing department of a furniture company for only six months when she met the biggest challenge of her career. His name was Mr. Aliyev, a senior manager who had worked in the company for twenty years. He was clever and experienced, but he had a habit of criticising other people in front of the whole team. More than once he told Shirin that her ideas were "childish".

At first, she tried to ignore him. She thought that if she worked harder, he would eventually respect her. But the situation got worse. During an important meeting in March, he interrupted her presentation and said that the figures were wrong. Shirin was embarrassed, and she almost cried in front of her colleagues. Later she discovered that her figures had been correct; Mr. Aliyev had simply used an old file.

That night she could not sleep. She considered resigning, but she needed the job and she liked the other people in her department. Instead, she asked her friend Jamshid, who had worked in human resources, for advice. Jamshid told her not to answer anger with anger. He suggested that she should ask Mr. Aliyev for a private conversation and speak calmly about specific problems, not about his character.

The next Monday, Shirin knocked on his door at four o'clock. She said, "I respect your experience, and I would like to learn from you. But when you criticise me in public, I cannot work well. Could we discuss my reports privately before the meetings?" Mr. Aliyev looked surprised. For a moment he said nothing, and then he admitted that he was under a lot of pressure because the company had lost an important customer.

Their relationship did not change overnight, but it improved. Mr. Aliyev started to check her work in his office, and he even praised her campaign for a new kitchen collection, which increased sales by fifteen percent. In June he recommended her for a small promotion.

Shirin often says that this experience taught her two things. First, people who behave badly are sometimes afraid. Second, it is much better to speak honestly and politely than to complain behind someone's back. She now helps new employees who have similar difficulties.

items.prompt: Where did Farhod and Nigora rent an apartment?
items.passage:
Farhod and his wife Nigora had wanted to buy their own flat since the day they got married. For five years they rented a small apartment on the outskirts of Andijan, and every month a large part of their income went to the owner. "We are paying for someone else's dream," Farhod often said. They tried to save money, but flat prices rose faster than their savings.

In the end, they decided to apply for a bank loan. The flat they liked cost three hundred and sixty million som. They had saved eighty million, which was more than twenty percent of the price, and the bank said that this was the minimum for a mortgage. The remaining amount would be paid back over fifteen years.

Before going to the bank, Farhod spent a week reading about different offers. He found that three banks had different interest rates, from nineteen to twenty-three percent. He also discovered that some banks charged extra fees which were not mentioned in the advertisements. He wrote everything down in a table and compared the total cost of each offer. "The lowest monthly payment is not always the cheapest loan," he explained to his wife.

They chose a state bank with an interest rate of nineteen percent. The application was long and tiring. They had to bring documents about their jobs, their income, and even their rental agreement. A bank officer called Mrs. Sultanova checked everything carefully and asked them several times whether they were sure that they could afford the monthly payment. Nigora admitted that she was a little frightened.

After three weeks, the bank approved the loan. On the day of signing, Farhod read each page slowly, even though the officer looked impatient. He wanted to be sure that he understood every condition, especially the rules about late payments.

They moved into their flat in October. It is not large, only two rooms and a kitchen, but it belongs to them, or at least it will in fifteen years. Every month they pay the instalment on the first day, and they have already decided not to buy anything unnecessary until the debt becomes smaller. "A loan is a promise," says Farhod. "You must keep it."

items.prompt: What does Aziza translate for?
items.passage:
Aziza used to work in an office, but three years ago she became a freelance translator. She translates documents from English and Russian into Uzbek, mostly for law firms and small businesses. Many people imagine that working for yourself means more freedom and less stress. Aziza says the truth is more complicated.

The biggest advantage, she says, is flexibility. She can start at seven in the morning, when her mind is fresh, and finish at two. In the afternoon she picks up her son from school and takes him to swimming lessons. When she worked in an office, she often saw her son for only an hour before bedtime. For her, this change alone was worth the risk.

However, there are disadvantages. A freelancer has no fixed salary. In some months Aziza earns eight million som, and in others only three. She learned this lesson in her first winter, when clients disappeared and she could hardly pay her rent. Since then she has kept an emergency fund equal to four months of expenses. She also sends a polite reminder to clients who do not pay on time, because sometimes people simply forget.

Another difficulty is finding new customers. At the beginning, she sent more than a hundred emails and received only five answers. She improved her profile on a professional website and asked satisfied clients to write short reviews. Soon, work started to come to her instead. Last year she translated a book about medicine, which took almost five months and brought her the highest payment of her career.

Aziza also had to learn discipline. At home there are many distractions, and nobody checks whether she is working. She uses a simple rule: she does not open social media before she has translated at least five pages. She also takes a short walk every two hours, which helps her concentrate.

When friends ask whether they should become freelancers, she answers carefully. "It is wonderful if you can plan your money and your time," she says. "If you cannot, you should stay in an office until you learn."

items.prompt: In which town is the bazaar?
items.passage:
The bazaar in Margilan opens before sunrise, and by six o'clock Rahim has already arranged his stall. He sells dried fruit and nuts: apricots, raisins, almonds and walnuts. He inherited the stall from his father, who had stood in the same place for thirty-five years. Rahim started to help him when he was only eleven, carrying heavy bags and weighing goods on an old metal scale.

According to Rahim, selling at a market is a skill that cannot be learned from books. The first rule is to be polite to everyone, even those who do not buy anything. A customer who leaves today may return tomorrow with five relatives. The second rule is to let people taste the goods. When a woman tries a sweet apricot, she rarely walks away without buying a kilo. The third rule is to remember prices. Wholesale prices change almost every week, and a trader who forgets this will soon lose money.

A normal day is long. In the morning, Rahim sells mainly to housewives and restaurant owners. Around noon, when the sun is strong, the market becomes quieter, and he takes a short rest in the shade and drinks green tea with the neighbouring traders. In the afternoon, tourists appear, and he sells small packages as gifts. He has learned a few words in English, French and Korean, which, he says, are worth more than any advertisement.

There are also difficult periods. Last summer a heavy rainstorm damaged part of his goods, and he lost nearly two million som. In winter, there are fewer customers because people travel less. To avoid risks, Rahim now sells through a messaging app as well, and he delivers orders to nearby towns twice a week.

At six in the evening he closes the stall and counts the money carefully. He writes the total in a small book, as his father did. Then he walks home, which takes ten minutes, and eats dinner with his three children.

"The market is not just a place for business," Rahim says. "It is where I learned how to talk to people, and that is more valuable than money."

items.prompt: How many applications had Jasur sent?
items.passage:
Last summer, Jasur was accepted for a two-month internship at an advertising agency in Tashkent. He was a second-year student of economics, and he had been applying for internships since January. He had sent forty applications and received only two invitations, so when the agency called him, he nearly jumped with joy.

The internship was unpaid, but the agency offered lunch and a monthly transport card. On the first day, a young manager called Dildora showed him around the office and introduced him to the team of twelve people. Jasur expected to make coffee and copy documents, which was what his cousin had done during his own internship. To his surprise, Dildora gave him a real task: to collect information about the habits of young customers for a new campaign for a juice company.

Jasur spent the first week reading reports and preparing a short survey. He asked eighty students from his university to answer the questions, and he discovered that most of them preferred drinks with less sugar. He presented the results at a team meeting, and his hands were shaking. Fortunately, nobody laughed. The director, Mr. Tursunov, said that the information was useful and asked a few difficult questions, which Jasur answered honestly, even when he did not know the answer.

Of course, he also made mistakes. In the third week he sent an email to the wrong client, and the agency had to apologise. Jasur was afraid that he would be dismissed. Instead, Dildora told him that everybody makes mistakes, and showed him a simple rule: check the name of the receiver twice before pressing "send".

At the end of the summer, the agency organised a small farewell party. Mr. Tursunov told Jasur that the juice company had used his idea of a low-sugar drink in its final campaign. He also offered him a part-time job for the autumn, with a real salary. Jasur accepted immediately.

Looking back, he says that the internship taught him more than a whole year at university. "At lectures, I learned theory," he explains. "At the agency, I learned how people actually work together."

items.prompt: How long has Bahrom been a taxi driver?
items.passage:
Bahrom has been a taxi driver in Tashkent for eleven years. Before that he worked as a mechanic, but the salary was low, and when his second daughter was born, he needed more income. A friend lent him a car, and he started to drive passengers. Today he has his own car, a white sedan which he looks after as carefully as a member of the family.

A typical working day for Bahrom begins at six in the morning. He checks the oil and the tyres, washes the windows, and drinks a cup of strong tea before he leaves. The first customers are usually people going to the airport or the railway station. Between nine and eleven the roads are full of traffic, and he sometimes spends half an hour in one place. He says that patience is the most important quality of a driver, more important than speed.

Since the arrival of ride-hailing apps, the work has changed a lot. Passengers can see the price in advance and give the driver a rating after the trip. Bahrom admits that at first he did not like this. The company takes about twenty percent of each fare, and drivers can be punished for a bad rating. However, he has also noticed advantages. He no longer waits for hours at the station, and he receives orders even at night.

He has met many interesting people in his car: a famous singer, a foreign doctor, and once a young couple who were hurrying to their own wedding. Bahrom drove so fast that he received a fine, but the couple arrived on time and invited him to the party. "That was the best fine I ever paid," he jokes.

The job is not easy. He works about twelve hours a day, six days a week, and his back often hurts. He also worries about the rising price of petrol. His dream is to save enough money to open a small car service with his brother, where he can use his old skills as a mechanic.

Nevertheless, he does not complain. "A driver sees the whole city every day," he says. "And every passenger has a story. I am paid to listen, too."

items.prompt: In which city was the workshop?
items.passage:
For forty years, Mr. Hamidov ran a small furniture workshop in Kokand. He had started it with two friends in 1985, and it slowly grew into a business with eighteen workers. The tables and chairs from his workshop could be found in schools, offices, and in thousands of homes across the country. Now he was sixty-eight, and it was time to decide who would continue the work.

He had two children. His son, Ilhom, lived in Dubai, where he worked as a manager in a hotel. His daughter, Mohira, had studied design and had worked in the workshop during her university holidays. Mr. Hamidov secretly hoped that she would take over, but he did not want to force anyone.

One evening in January, the whole family gathered for dinner. Mr. Hamidov explained that his health was no longer good and that he wanted to retire by the end of the year. To his surprise, Mohira had already prepared a plan. She said that she loved the workshop, but she believed that it needed to change. The old catalogue was out of date, the workshop had no website, and young customers were buying cheap furniture from abroad.

Mr. Hamidov was worried. He had always done things in the traditional way, and he feared that changes might ruin the quality. Mohira promised that the quality would not change. She suggested that they should keep the best traditional designs and add a modern line made from the same wood. She also wanted to sell through the internet and to offer delivery to other cities.

They agreed on a trial period of six months, during which Mr. Hamidov would remain as an adviser. The new collection was ready in June, and the first online orders came within a week. By September, sales had risen by thirty percent, and Mohira had hired three new workers. Her father, who had been the most doubtful, was now the first to show customers the new chairs.

In December, the family organised a small ceremony in the workshop. Mr. Hamidov gave his daughter the keys and said, "I built the workshop with my hands. You will build its future with your head." Ilhom, who had flown in from Dubai, promised to help with advertising abroad.

items.prompt: How old was Dilnoza when she fell into the river?
items.passage:
Dilnoza Karimova had been afraid of deep water since she was seven years old, when she fell into a river near her grandmother's village in Fergana. For almost thirty years she had avoided swimming pools, beaches and even boat trips. Then, in January, her doctor told her that her back problems would improve if she found a gentle form of exercise. He suggested swimming, and Dilnoza, who was thirty-four at the time, felt her stomach turn. However, she decided that if she did not face her fear now, she never would.

She found an adult beginners' class at a pool in Tashkent that ran on Tuesday and Thursday evenings at half past six. The teacher, a patient man named Rustam, had taught more than two hundred adults to swim. On the first evening, he did not ask anyone to get into the water at all. Instead, the group sat on the edge of the pool and put their feet in. Rustam explained that most adults are not afraid of water itself but of losing control, and that the first skill to learn is simply to breathe calmly.

The next three weeks were difficult. Dilnoza practised blowing bubbles, floating on her back with a foam board and kicking while holding the wall. Twice she nearly gave up, and once she cried in the changing room because the other students seemed to be progressing faster. Rustam told her that if she had compared herself with the others, she would have felt worse, and that she should only compare herself with the person she had been last week. This advice helped her more than any technique.

In the sixth week something changed. Rustam asked her to push off from the wall and glide, and she travelled almost four metres without touching the bottom. She was so surprised that she swallowed some water and coughed for a minute, but she was also smiling. By the end of March she could swim a full length of twenty-five metres, and by June she was swimming thirty minutes without stopping. Her back pain had almost disappeared.

Today Dilnoza swims three mornings a week before work. She says the biggest lesson was not about swimming at all. It was the discovery that a fear which has lasted for decades can be reduced step by step. Next summer she plans to swim in a lake with her nephew, who is nine and has been teasing her about being a slow learner.

Dilnoza Karimova had been afraid of deep water since she was seven years old, when she fell into a river near her grandmother's village in Fergana. For almost thirty years she had avoided swimming pools, beaches and even boat trips. Then, in January, her doctor told her that her back problems would improve if she found a gentle form of exercise. She found an adult beginners' class at a pool in Tashkent that ran on Tuesday and Thursday evenings at half past six. The teacher, a patient man named Rustam, had taught more than two hundred adults to swim. On the first evening, he did not ask anyone to get into the water at all. Twice she nearly gave up, and once she cried in the changing room because the other students seemed to be progressing faster. items.prompt: Who challenged Bobur to run the marathon?
items.passage:
Bobur Yusupov never imagined that he would run a marathon. At school he had been the boy who hid at the back during sports lessons, and by the age of thirty he weighed ninety-eight kilograms and got out of breath climbing two flights of stairs. Everything changed when his younger sister, Madina, challenged him to run the Samarkand marathon with her. He laughed at first, but when she offered to train with him every Saturday, he finally agreed. The race was eight months away.

Their plan was simple. During the first month they only walked and jogged for twenty minutes, three times a week. Bobur's knees hurt and his shoes were the wrong size, so he visited a specialist shop where a young assistant watched him run on a treadmill and recommended a different pair. After the third month they were running ten kilometres on Saturdays. Madina insisted that they must never increase the weekly distance by more than ten percent, because she had read that this rule prevents injuries. Bobur had not believed her until a friend who ignored the rule had to stop for six weeks.

The hardest part was not the running but the food. Bobur loved fried dumplings and sweet tea with three spoons of sugar. He did not give up his favourite dishes completely, but he started eating them only on Sundays. He also learned to drink water regularly, even when he did not feel thirsty. By the day of the race he had lost fourteen kilograms and felt stronger than he had ever felt in his life.

The marathon took place on a cool morning in October. More than three thousand people stood at the start line in Registan Square, and Bobur felt both excited and terrified. The first twenty kilometres passed easily because crowds were cheering and children offered the runners slices of orange. Around the thirty-second kilometre, however, his legs became heavy and he wanted to stop. Madina ran beside him and talked about silly things until he forgot the pain.

They crossed the finish line in five hours and eleven minutes. It was not a fast time, but Bobur cried when the medal was put around his neck. He says that if he had known how hard it would be, he might never have started, and that is exactly why he is glad nobody told him. This autumn he is training for a half marathon in Bukhara.

items.prompt: What could Aziza cook before the class?
items.answer: Only boiled eggs and plain rice
items.passage:
When Aziza Rakhimova moved to London to study, she realised that she could not cook anything except boiled eggs and plain rice. At home in Namangan, her mother had always prepared the meals, and Aziza had never been allowed to help because the kitchen was considered too small for two people. After three weeks of eating cheap sandwiches and instant noodles, she felt tired and unhealthy, so she decided to sign up for a cooking class near her university.

The class took place every Wednesday evening in a bright kitchen above a bakery. There were twelve students, ranging from a retired engineer named Walter to a nervous teenager called Priya. The chef, a cheerful woman from Naples named Chiara, began the first lesson by saying that cooking is not magic. According to her, anyone can make a good meal if they have fresh ingredients, a sharp knife and a little patience. She then showed them how to hold a knife properly, and Aziza cut her first onion without crying, which she considered a small victory.

Over the following six weeks the group learned to make tomato soup, fresh pasta, roast chicken with vegetables, a spicy lentil stew, a lemon cake and, finally, a traditional pilaf which Aziza was asked to demonstrate. Everyone was surprised at how well she managed to season the rice, and Chiara admitted that she had never tasted such a perfect carrot. Aziza explained that her grandmother used to say the secret was to cut the carrots in long, thin strips and never to stir the rice too early.

The most valuable lesson, though, was about planning. Chiara taught the students to write a weekly menu, to buy vegetables at the market on Saturdays and to cook large portions that could be frozen. Aziza now spends around forty pounds a week on food, which is about half of what she used to spend on ready meals. She also invites her classmates for dinner on Fridays, and last month she cooked for eight people in her tiny flat.

When she phoned her mother to tell her about the dinner, her mother was silent for a moment and then asked for the lemon cake recipe. Aziza laughed, because she realised that for the first time in her life she was teaching her mother something in the kitchen.
options: Only boiled eggs and plain rice

items.prompt: What was Jasur's job?
items.passage:
Jasur Tursunov, a twenty-six-year-old software developer, used to think that sleep was a waste of time. He regularly worked until three in the morning, drank four cups of coffee a day and woke up at seven to start again. For two years he believed that he was simply an energetic person who did not need much rest. Then one Tuesday he fell asleep during an important meeting, and his manager, who was not angry but worried, suggested that he should see a sleep specialist.

The specialist, Dr Nigora Saidova, asked him to keep a sleep diary for two weeks. The results were shocking. Jasur slept on average only five hours a night, and at weekends he slept for twelve hours to make up for it. Dr Saidova explained that this pattern, which she called social jet lag, confuses the body clock and makes people feel as if they were travelling across time zones every week. She added that sleeping badly for a long time increases the risk of heart problems and weakens the memory.

She gave him a series of simple rules. First, he had to go to bed and get up at the same time every day, even on Sundays. Second, he should stop drinking coffee after two in the afternoon, since caffeine stays in the body for up to eight hours. Third, he must switch off his laptop and phone an hour before bedtime, because the blue light from screens tells the brain that it is still daytime. Finally, the bedroom should be cool, dark and quiet.

The first week was terrible. Jasur lay awake until two o'clock and felt irritable the next morning. He nearly returned to his old habits, but his sister encouraged him to continue. After ten days, he started to fall asleep within twenty minutes, and by the end of the month he was sleeping seven and a half hours every night. To his surprise, he finished his programming tasks faster than before and made fewer mistakes.

Nowadays Jasur goes to bed at eleven thirty and gets up at seven. He still enjoys working late occasionally, but he never does it twice in a row. He jokes that he has become a boring person, although he admits that he has never felt better.

items.prompt: Why did Hamid start the football team?
items.answer: Many teenagers had nothing to do and the club was too expensive
items.passage:
In the town of Kokand, a retired schoolteacher named Hamid Ismoilov started a free football team for teenagers eight years ago. He had noticed that many boys and girls in his neighbourhood spent their afternoons sitting in front of phones or wandering aimlessly in the streets. The local sports club charged high fees, and many families simply could not afford them. So Hamid took an old ball, borrowed two goalposts from a nearby school and invited anyone who wanted to play to come to the empty field behind his house.

On the first Saturday only five boys appeared. By the end of the year there were forty-two players, divided into three age groups. Hamid did not have any official training in coaching, but he read books, watched videos and asked a friend who had once played for a professional club to give advice. His main rule was that nobody sits on the bench for the whole game. Even the weakest player must play for at least twenty minutes, because, as he says, confidence cannot be built from the side of the pitch.

Hamid also insists that his players keep up with their school work. Every Thursday afternoon, the team meets at the local library, where volunteer students help with homework. A boy who fails an exam is not punished, but he has to spend extra time studying before the next match. Over the years, parents have reported that their children's marks have improved and that they behave more politely at home.

The team, called Kokand Stars, has also achieved some real sporting success. Two years ago it won the regional youth tournament, beating a team from Andijan four to three in a dramatic final. Three former players now play for professional clubs, and one of them, a defender named Sardor, sends money every year to buy new uniforms. Not everyone has become a footballer, of course. Another former student is now a doctor, and he says that the team taught him to work with others under pressure.

This year, the town council has finally offered Hamid a proper stadium with a grass pitch and changing rooms. He accepted with gratitude but said he would continue to use the old field on Saturdays, because that is where the story began.
