items.prompt: What was Malika's job?
items.passage:
Last January, Malika Sobirova, a nurse from Andijan, made an unusual New Year's resolution. She decided to stop eating meat for twelve months. Malika was not worried about animals, at least not at the beginning. Her main reason was health. Her father had suffered a heart attack at fifty-two, and her doctor had warned her that she was likely to have the same problem if she did not change her diet. Her family, who ate meat at almost every meal, thought the idea was ridiculous.

The first month was the most difficult. In Uzbekistan, a meal without meat can seem almost impossible, and Malika was surprised how many traditional dishes contain it. At family weddings she found herself eating bread, salad and plain rice while her cousins enjoyed large plates of kebab. She also felt hungry and weak in the second week, which she later understood was because she had not replaced the meat with enough other protein. A friend who studied nutrition advised her to eat more beans, lentils, nuts and eggs.

After that, things improved. Malika discovered that Uzbek cuisine offers more vegetarian dishes than she had thought. She started cooking lentil soup, stuffed peppers and a pumpkin dish called kadu oshi, and she learned to love chickpeas in every possible form. Her sister, who had made fun of the experiment, secretly asked for the lentil soup recipe in April. By June, Malika had lost six kilograms and her cholesterol level, which her doctor measured every three months, had fallen by almost twenty percent.

There were social difficulties as well. Some colleagues made jokes, and a few relatives took her choice as a criticism of their own habits. Malika learned to explain her decision calmly and never to lecture others. She says that nothing makes people defend meat more strongly than being told that they should stop eating it.

When December arrived, Malika had to decide whether to return to meat. She chose a compromise. She now eats fish twice a week and meat only on special occasions, but she still cooks vegetarian food at home. Her father, inspired by her results, has also started eating more vegetables and takes a daily walk of forty minutes.

Her father had suffered a heart attack at fifty-two, and her doctor had warned her that she was likely to have the same problem if she did not change her diet. Her family, who ate meat at almost every meal, thought the idea was ridiculous.

The first month was the most difficult. In Uzbekistan, a meal without meat can seem almost impossible, and Malika was surprised how many traditional dishes contain it. At family weddings she found herself eating bread, salad and plain rice while her cousins enjoyed large plates of kebab. She also felt hungry and weak in the second week, which she later understood was because she had not replaced the meat with enough other protein. A friend who studied nutrition advised her to eat more beans, lentils, nuts and eggs.

After that, things improved. Malika discovered that Uzbek cuisine offers more vegetarian dishes than she had thought. She started cooking lentil soup, stuffed peppers and a pumpkin dish called kadu oshi, and she learned to love chickpeas in every possible form. Her sister, who had made fun of the experiment, secretly asked for the lentil soup recipe in April. By June, Malika had lost six kilograms and her cholesterol level, which her doctor measured every three months, had fallen by almost twenty percent.

There were social difficulties as well. Some colleagues made jokes, and a few relatives took her choice as a criticism of their own habits. Malika learned to explain her decision calmly and never to lecture others. She says that nothing makes people defend meat more strongly than being told that they should stop eating it.

When December arrived, Malika had to decide whether to return to meat. She chose a compromise. She now eats fish twice a week and meat only on special occasions, but she still cooks vegetarian food at home. Her father, inspired by her results, has also started eating more vegetables and takes a daily walk of forty minutes.

items.prompt: What time does the morning class start?
items.passage:
Every morning at six thirty, a small group of people gathers on the roof of an old apartment building in the centre of Tashkent. They roll out their mats between flower pots and satellite dishes, and for an hour they follow the instructions of a calm voice. The voice belongs to Gulnora Azimova, a thirty-nine-year-old former accountant who changed her career completely after she discovered yoga during a difficult period of her life.

Gulnora's story began six years ago. She was working twelve hours a day, sleeping badly and suffering from constant headaches. A colleague invited her to a free introductory lesson, and Gulnora agreed mainly to be polite. She was sure that yoga was only for young, flexible people. In fact, the instructor was a woman of sixty, and she could stand on her head. Gulnora was impressed and went back the next week. Within three months, her headaches had almost disappeared.

After two years of practising, Gulnora took a teacher's course in Rishikesh, India, which lasted a month and cost most of her savings. When she came back, she left her job, which shocked her parents. They had hoped that their daughter would have a safe, respectable career. She started teaching in a rented room, but there were few students at first. The idea of the rooftop came from a neighbour who had a key to the building and noticed that Gulnora was practising on her balcony.

The rooftop classes are now so popular that there is a waiting list. Gulnora charges only a small fee and gives one free lesson a month for people who cannot pay. Her students include a taxi driver, a university professor and a seventy-year-old grandmother who says that she can finally touch her knees. In winter the group moves to a heated room on the ground floor, although many students complain that they miss the sunrise.

When asked what she tells beginners, Gulnora says that yoga is not about touching your toes. It is about learning to listen to your body without judging it. She adds, smiling, that her parents have now joined the Saturday class, and her father is more flexible than she expected.

items.prompt: What did Mrs Haydarova notice in the rubbish bins?
items.answer: More than half of the food had been thrown away
items.passage:
When the headteacher of School Number Forty-Two in Samarkand, Mrs Shirin Haydarova, looked at the rubbish bins after lunch, she was shocked. More than half of the food that the pupils received had been thrown away. The soup was cold, the vegetables were overcooked and many children preferred to buy crisps and sweet drinks from the shop across the road. She decided that something had to change, and in September she started a one-year experiment to improve the school lunch.

The first step was to ask the pupils what they wanted. Questionnaires were given to all four hundred and twenty children, and the results were surprising. Most of them did not dislike healthy food. They complained about the lack of choice, the long queue and the fact that lunch lasted only fifteen minutes. A small group of older students formed a food committee and met the cook, Mr Anvar, every Friday to discuss the menu for the following week.

Several changes were introduced. Lunch was extended to thirty minutes. A salad bar was added where pupils could choose their own vegetables, and fruit replaced cakes as the usual dessert. Mr Anvar also began to buy tomatoes, cucumbers and herbs from local farmers instead of a distant supplier, which made the food fresher and, unexpectedly, cheaper. The sweet drinks were removed from the school shop and replaced by water and fresh juice.

At first there was resistance. Some parents complained that their children would starve, and a few pupils brought their own sandwiches in protest. However, after about six weeks the situation began to change. Food waste fell by sixty percent, and teachers reported that pupils were more attentive in the afternoon lessons. The school nurse noticed that visits from children complaining of stomach aches had decreased noticeably.

At the end of the year, the experiment was considered so successful that the city education department invited Mrs Haydarova to present her results to other headteachers. She told them that the most important ingredient was not money but listening. If children are involved in the decision, she said, they are far more likely to eat what is on their plate.

When the headteacher of School Number Forty-Two in Samarkand, Mrs Shirin Haydarova, looked at the rubbish bins after lunch, she was shocked. More than half of the food that the pupils received had been thrown away. The soup was cold, the vegetables were overcooked and many children preferred to buy crisps and sweet drinks from the shop across the road. She decided that something had to change, and in September she started a one-year experiment to improve the school lunch.

The first step was to ask the pupils what they wanted. Questionnaires were given to all four hundred and twenty children, and the results were surprising. Most of them did not dislike healthy food. They complained about the lack of choice, the long queue and the fact that lunch lasted only fifteen minutes. A small group of older students formed a food committee and met the cook, Mr Anvar, every Friday to discuss the menu for the following week.

Several changes were introduced. Lunch was extended to thirty minutes. A salad bar was added where pupils could choose their own vegetables, and fruit replaced cakes as the usual dessert. Mr Anvar also began to buy tomatoes, cucumbers and herbs from local farmers instead of a distant supplier, which made the food fresher and, unexpectedly, cheaper. The sweet drinks were removed from the school shop and replaced by water and fresh juice.

At first there was resistance. Some parents complained that their children would starve, and a few pupils brought their own sandwiches in protest. However, after about six weeks the situation began to change. Food waste fell by sixty percent, and teachers reported that pupils were more attentive in the afternoon lessons. The school nurse noticed that visits from children complaining of stomach aches had decreased noticeably.

At the end of the year, the experiment was considered so successful that the city education department invited Mrs Haydarova to present her results to other headteachers. She told them that the most important ingredient was not money but listening. If children are involved in the decision, she said, they are far more likely to eat what is on their plate.

items.prompt: How did Sevara hurt her knee?
items.answer: She landed awkwardly after jumping to block the ball
items.passage:
Sevara Normatova was nineteen years old and one of the best volleyball players in her university when she tore a ligament in her knee during a match against a team from Bukhara. She remembers the moment clearly. She jumped to block the ball, landed awkwardly and heard a small, sharp sound, like a stick breaking. By the time the ambulance arrived, her knee had swollen to the size of a melon. The doctor told her that she would need an operation and at least eight months of rehabilitation.

The operation took place ten days later and went well. Nevertheless, the following weeks were the hardest of Sevara's life. She could not walk without crutches and was forced to give up her team, her friends' company and the routine that had defined her days since childhood. She felt sad and sometimes angry, and she admits that she spent a few evenings doing nothing but watching old matches on her phone. Her physiotherapist, a firm but kind man named Eldor, noticed her mood and told her that mental recovery is as important as physical recovery.

Eldor gave her a clear programme. In the first month she did gentle exercises lying down, such as lifting the leg and bending the knee. In the second month she began to use an exercise bike, and in the fourth month she was allowed to swim. He told her never to skip a session, but also never to do more than he recommended. Sevara admits that she broke this rule once, trying to run too early, and the knee was sore for a week.

To stay connected to the sport, she started helping the university coach by recording matches and analysing the opponents' tactics. She was surprised to find that she enjoyed it, and her notes helped the team reach the semi-final. In the eighth month, she returned to training with a special brace and, in the tenth month, played her first full match.

Today Sevara says that the injury taught her patience. She also decided to study sports medicine, so that she can help other athletes, and she gives one piece of advice to every young player she meets. Warm up properly, even if you are late for the game.
options: She landed awkwardly after jumping to block the ball

items.prompt: How far was Otabek's office from his apartment?
items.passage:
Until last spring, Otabek Mirzayev drove to work every day. His office was only seven kilometres from his apartment, but the journey took forty minutes in heavy traffic and cost him a fortune in petrol. He also spent most of the day sitting, first in his car and then at his desk, and he had started to feel stiff and tired. When his company announced a scheme which offered employees a cheap loan to buy a bicycle, he decided to try it, although he had not ridden a bike since he was a teenager.

He bought a simple grey bicycle with a basket and a good lock. His wife, Zilola, who often cycled with their children on Sundays, gave him a few lessons in a quiet park to help him regain his balance. At first he wobbled dangerously and, in the second lesson, fell into a bush while the children laughed. After a week, however, he felt confident enough to try the route to work early on a Saturday morning when the streets were empty.

The first official working day on the bike was a revelation. The journey took only twenty-five minutes because he could use a path along a canal and avoid the congested main road. He arrived with a slight headache from the unfamiliar effort but also with a clear mind. Over the following weeks, he learned several practical lessons. He bought a helmet and a bright jacket, after a taxi nearly hit him. He kept a spare shirt in the office because he sweated in warm weather. And he checked the weather forecast every evening, since rain made the paths dangerously slippery.

The results after six months were impressive. Otabek had lost five kilograms, his blood pressure was lower, and he had saved enough money on fuel to pay for the bicycle twice. Two colleagues, inspired by his example, also started cycling, and now the three of them ride together every Wednesday.

Otabek admits that cycling is not perfect in every situation. In January, when the temperature fell to minus eight, he returned to the car for two weeks. Nevertheless, he is convinced that he will never go back to driving every day.

items.prompt: Who led the study?
items.passage:
Breakfast is often described as the most important meal of the day, but what people actually eat in the morning varies enormously from country to country. A recent study by a group of nutritionists, led by Professor Kamola Ergasheva, compared the breakfasts of families in six countries and tried to discover which habits were really good for health. The results, which were published in a university magazine, were more complicated than many people had expected.

In Japan, the typical breakfast includes rice, grilled fish, a bowl of soup and pickled vegetables. It contains little sugar and a lot of protein, and the researchers found that Japanese children who ate it regularly concentrated better at school. In Turkey, a table is often covered with olives, cheese, tomatoes, cucumbers, eggs and fresh bread. Families sit together for at least thirty minutes, and Professor Ergasheva believes that the social part of the meal is almost as valuable as the food.

The situation in other places was less encouraging. In the United Kingdom and the United States, many children start the day with sweet cereal, which can contain as much sugar as a chocolate bar. In some parts of Central Asia, a quick breakfast of tea with white bread and jam is common, because mornings are busy and people say that they have no time to cook. The researchers do not criticise these families but note that the meal gives energy for only an hour or two.

Professor Ergasheva's team also tested the claim that skipping breakfast always makes people gain weight. They found that the answer depends on the person. Some adults who skipped breakfast ate more at lunch and dinner, while others managed perfectly well. The only group that clearly suffered from missing the morning meal was children under twelve, who were less attentive and more irritable before midday.

The researchers conclude with three suggestions. First, include some protein, such as eggs, yoghurt or beans. Second, choose whole grains instead of white flour. Third, eat with other people when it is possible. According to the professor, none of these changes is expensive, and all of them can be introduced slowly, one morning at a time.

items.prompt: Whose idea was the hiking trip?
items.passage:
Last June, a group of eight friends from Tashkent decided to spend a weekend hiking in the Chimgan mountains. The idea came from Akmal, a geography teacher who had been to the area many times and promised that the views were worth the effort. Most of the group were beginners, and the only woman with serious experience was Laylo, who had once climbed a peak of four thousand metres. Everyone agreed to meet at the bus station at six on Saturday morning.

The preparation had started a week earlier. Laylo sent the group a list of things to bring, and she was strict about it. Each person needed comfortable boots, a warm jacket, a waterproof coat, two litres of water, a hat and sunscreen. She advised them not to carry heavy bags, because every extra kilogram feels like five after several hours of climbing. Dilshod, the youngest member, ignored her advice and packed a large tin of fruit, which became a joke for the rest of the trip.

The first day's route was about twelve kilometres long and climbed from fifteen hundred to twenty-three hundred metres. The weather was sunny, and the group stopped three times for rest. Around noon, they reached a small waterfall and ate lunch beside it. In the afternoon, however, Dilshod's boot began to hurt his heel, and Akmal showed him how to use a plaster and change his socks. They arrived at their campsite at five o'clock, tired but happy, and cooked soup on a small gas stove.

That night, the temperature dropped to four degrees, and several people could not sleep because of the cold. Nobody complained, though, because the sky was full of stars brighter than any of them had ever seen in the city. In the morning, they climbed for another hour to a rocky ridge and enjoyed a view over the snowy peaks while they drank hot tea.

The journey home was quiet, as most people fell asleep on the bus. When they arrived back in Tashkent, Laylo asked whether anyone wanted to repeat the trip in the autumn. Eight hands went up immediately, and Dilshod promised to bring a bigger tin.

Around noon, they reached a small waterfall and ate lunch beside it. In the afternoon, however, Dilshod's boot began to hurt his heel, and Akmal showed him how to use a plaster and change his socks. They arrived at their campsite at five o'clock, tired but happy, and cooked soup on a small gas stove.

That night, the temperature dropped to four degrees, and several people could not sleep because of the cold. Nobody complained, though, because the sky was full of stars brighter than any of them had ever seen in the city. In the morning, they climbed for another hour to a rocky ridge and enjoyed a view over the snowy peaks while they drank hot tea.

The journey home was quiet, as most people fell asleep on the bus. When they arrived back in Tashkent, Laylo asked whether anyone wanted to repeat the trip in the autumn. Eight hands went up immediately, and Dilshod promised to bring a bigger tin.

items.prompt: What was Feruza's job?
items.passage:
Many people know that they should drink more water, but few of them actually do it. Feruza Abdullaeva, a school librarian in Karshi, was one of those people. For years she drank two cups of tea in the morning, a coffee in the afternoon and almost nothing else. She often had headaches around three o'clock and felt sleepy during the last lessons. It never occurred to her that the reason might be as simple as a lack of water, until a visiting nurse gave a talk at her school.

The nurse explained that the human body is about sixty percent water and that even mild dehydration can cause tiredness, headaches and difficulty concentrating. She said that most adults need about two litres of fluid a day, though the exact amount depends on the weather, physical activity and body size. A useful sign, she added, is the colour of urine. If it is pale yellow, the person is probably drinking enough, but if it is dark, it is time to have a glass of water.

Feruza decided to run a personal experiment for one month. She bought a one-litre bottle and a set of rubber bands. Her plan was to fill the bottle twice a day and drink it all before dinner. At first she forgot constantly, so she set an alarm on her phone for ten o'clock, noon, three o'clock and five o'clock. She also made the water more attractive by adding slices of lemon or cucumber, since she thought that plain water was boring.

The results arrived faster than she had expected. After five days, her afternoon headaches had disappeared. After two weeks, a colleague commented that her skin looked healthier. By the end of the month, she had also reduced her coffee to one cup a day, which she had not planned at all. She felt less hungry between meals, which she explained by the fact that thirst is sometimes confused with hunger.

Feruza now shares her bottle trick with her pupils. She keeps a poster in the library with the question, Have you had any water today, and she says that the children are more willing to listen than the adults. Her only complaint is that she now visits the bathroom more often than before.

items.prompt: How old is Karim Nazarov?
items.passage:
At eighty-one, Karim Nazarov walks six kilometres every morning, and his neighbours in Margilan set their watches by him. He leaves his house at exactly five forty-five, wearing the same grey cap and carrying a wooden stick which he rarely uses. His grandson, Temur, who is a journalist, became curious about this habit and decided to spend a week walking with his grandfather in order to write an article about it.

On the first morning, Temur expected to find a slow old man and was surprised by the speed. They walked past the bazaar, along the river and through a small park where Karim greeted every person by name. Karim explained that he began to walk after he retired from the silk factory at sixty, because he did not know what to do with his time. His wife had been ill then, and the doctor had advised him to find a way to reduce stress. A short walk became a long walk, and the long walk became a habit that he had kept for twenty-one years.

During the week, Temur discovered that the walk was about much more than exercise. It was also a social event. Karim stopped to talk to the baker, who gave him a warm piece of bread, to a group of old men who played chess on a bench, and to a young mother who asked for advice about her sick child. He seemed to know everybody, and everybody seemed glad to see him. Temur realised that his grandfather had built a community around the habit.

Karim has a few simple rules. He never takes his phone, because he says that it spoils the silence. He drinks a glass of water before leaving and eats a handful of walnuts after returning. He walks in all weathers except heavy rain, and in winter he wears two pairs of socks. He also believes that a person should never walk alone for too long, which is why he often invites neighbours to join him.

When the article was published, it was shared thousands of times online. Temur received messages from readers in several countries, and some of them asked whether his grandfather would be willing to lead a walking club. Karim, when he heard about it, laughed and said that he was too busy walking.

items.prompt: How long has Dr Qodirova worked with students?
items.passage:
Every year in May and June, university students in Uzbekistan face the same problem. Exams arrive, nights become shorter and healthy habits are the first thing to disappear. Dr Zarina Qodirova, who works at the student health centre at the National University, has watched this pattern for fifteen years. She says that the students who perform best in exams are not necessarily those who study the longest, but those who look after their bodies while they study.

According to Dr Qodirova, the most common mistake is to sacrifice sleep. Students believe that an extra three hours of study at night will help them remember more facts, but research shows the opposite. During sleep, the brain organises what it has learned, and without it, information is quickly forgotten. She recommends at least seven hours a night, and she advises students never to study in the last hour before bed, because the mind needs time to relax.

The second mistake is poor food. Students living in dormitories often survive on energy drinks, biscuits and instant noodles, which give a sudden burst of energy followed by tiredness. Dr Qodirova suggests simple alternatives, such as bananas, nuts, boiled eggs and brown bread, which release energy slowly. She also recommends keeping a bottle of water on the desk, because even slight dehydration reduces concentration.

Physical activity is the third element. Many students stay at their desks for ten hours without moving. Dr Qodirova suggests a ten-minute walk every two hours and a longer walk or some light sport once a day. This does not take time away from studying, she says, because it improves blood flow to the brain and reduces anxiety. At her centre, she also runs a free breathing class every Tuesday at four, which more than sixty students attended last year.

Finally, she reminds students that it is acceptable to ask for help. Stress before exams is normal, but if a student cannot sleep for several nights, feels panic or loses appetite completely, it is time to talk to a doctor or a counsellor. Dr Qodirova ends her advice with a sentence that she often repeats. An exam measures what you know today, not who you are.

items.prompt: How many times a day had Dilnoza unlocked her phone?
items.passage:
When Dilnoza Karimova, a nineteen-year-old student from Samarkand, counted how often she touched her phone, she could not believe the result. An app on her screen showed that she had unlocked it one hundred and eighty times in a single day. She had never thought of herself as an addict, but the numbers made her feel uncomfortable, and she decided to find out what was happening.

Researchers say that Dilnoza is not unusual. A study carried out at a university in Tashkent last year followed four hundred young people for three months. The scientists discovered that the average student spent five and a half hours a day on a phone. Many of them said that they checked their messages even when nothing had rung or buzzed. If the phone was out of sight, they felt nervous, and some had trouble concentrating on lessons.

Dilnoza decided to experiment. First, she turned off all notifications except calls from her family. Then she bought an old alarm clock, so that her phone no longer had to sleep next to her bed. She had often looked at videos until two in the morning, and she had always woken up tired. After a week of the new routine, she was going to bed at eleven and feeling much more awake in the morning.

The hardest part was lunchtime. Her friends were used to taking photos of their food and sharing them immediately, and at first they laughed at her. However, after two weeks, her friend Aziz admitted that he had started to feel the same way. Together they made a rule: the first person to touch a phone during a meal would pay for everyone's tea. Aziz lost the game three times in the first week.

Doctors do not tell people to throw their phones away. Dr. Malika Rustamova, who led the Tashkent study, explains that phones are useful tools, and that the problem is only the habit of checking them without thinking. She suggests keeping the phone in another room while studying and setting a daily limit of three hours. Dilnoza now spends about two hours a day on her phone, and she says she has finished more books this year than in the previous five years.

items.prompt: How many young people took part in the Tashkent study?
items.passage:
When Dilnoza Karimova, a nineteen-year-old student from Samarkand, counted how often she touched her phone, she could not believe the result. An app on her screen showed that she had unlocked it one hundred and eighty times in a single day. She had never thought of herself as an addict, but the numbers made her feel uncomfortable, and she decided to find out what was happening.

Researchers say that Dilnoza is not unusual. A study carried out at a university in Tashkent last year followed four hundred young people for three months. The scientists discovered that the average student spent five and a half hours a day on a phone. Many of them said that they checked their messages even when nothing had rung or buzzed. If the phone was out of sight, they felt nervous, and some had trouble concentrating on lessons.

Dilnoza decided to experiment. First, she turned off all notifications except calls from her family. Then she bought an old alarm clock, so that her phone no longer had to sleep next to her bed. She had often looked at videos until two in the morning, and she had always woken up tired. After a week of the new routine, she was going to bed at eleven and feeling much more awake in the morning.

The hardest part was lunchtime. Her friends were used to taking photos of their food and sharing them immediately, and at first they laughed at her. However, after two weeks, her friend Aziz admitted that he had started to feel the same way. Together they made a rule: the first person to touch a phone during a meal would pay for everyone's tea. Aziz lost the game three times in the first week.

Doctors do not tell people to throw their phones away. Dr. Malika Rustamova, who led the Tashkent study, explains that phones are useful tools, and that the problem is only the habit of checking them without thinking. She suggests keeping the phone in another room while studying and setting a daily limit of three hours. Dilnoza now spends about two hours a day on her phone, and she says she has finished more books this year than in the previous five years.

items.prompt: In which city is the hospital?
items.passage:
At the City Children's Hospital in Bukhara, a new member of staff started work in March. It is a white robot called Nuri, about the height of a ten-year-old child, and it has two large blue eyes on a round screen. Nuri does not give medicine and it does not perform operations. Its job is to carry food, bring blankets and, most importantly, keep young patients company.

The idea came from a nurse named Gulnora Saidova. She had noticed that many children were frightened when they arrived at the hospital. They missed their parents, they disliked the smell of the corridors, and they refused to eat. Gulnora read about a similar robot in a hospital in Japan, and she wrote a long letter to the hospital director. After six months of discussion, the hospital agreed to buy one machine as a test.

Nuri can speak three languages: Uzbek, Russian and English. It tells jokes, sings short songs and plays simple games, such as guessing which hand hides a small coin. When a child is crying, it uses its sensors to notice the sad face and says quietly, "Would you like to hear a story?" Nurses say that the effect is almost magical. A seven-year-old boy named Timur, who had not spoken for two days after his operation, started laughing at the robot's dancing.

Of course, some doctors were worried at first. They feared that the robot might replace nurses, or that it would make mistakes with the equipment. Dr. Farhod Aliyev explained that these fears were not realistic. Nuri is controlled by a program that only allows it to move on a fixed route, and it is never left alone with a child for more than fifteen minutes. A nurse always watches the screen in the main office.

After eight months, the hospital measured the results. The number of children who finished their meals had risen by almost thirty percent, and parents reported that their sons and daughters were calmer before treatment. The director has now asked for two more robots, which are expected to arrive next spring. Gulnora says that the best part of her job is hearing children say goodbye to Nuri at the door.

items.prompt: The hospital wants to get more robots.
items.passage:
At the City Children's Hospital in Bukhara, a new member of staff started work in March. It is a white robot called Nuri, about the height of a ten-year-old child, and it has two large blue eyes on a round screen. Nuri does not give medicine and it does not perform operations. Its job is to carry food, bring blankets and, most importantly, keep young patients company.

The idea came from a nurse named Gulnora Saidova. She had noticed that many children were frightened when they arrived at the hospital. They missed their parents, they disliked the smell of the corridors, and they refused to eat. Gulnora read about a similar robot in a hospital in Japan, and she wrote a long letter to the hospital director. After six months of discussion, the hospital agreed to buy one machine as a test.

Nuri can speak three languages: Uzbek, Russian and English. It tells jokes, sings short songs and plays simple games, such as guessing which hand hides a small coin. When a child is crying, it uses its sensors to notice the sad face and says quietly, "Would you like to hear a story?" Nurses say that the effect is almost magical. A seven-year-old boy named Timur, who had not spoken for two days after his operation, started laughing at the robot's dancing.

Of course, some doctors were worried at first. They feared that the robot might replace nurses, or that it would make mistakes with the equipment. Dr. Farhod Aliyev explained that these fears were not realistic. Nuri is controlled by a program that only allows it to move on a fixed route, and it is never left alone with a child for more than fifteen minutes. A nurse always watches the screen in the main office.

After eight months, the hospital measured the results. The number of children who finished their meals had risen by almost thirty percent, and parents reported that their sons and daughters were calmer before treatment. The director has now asked for two more robots, which are expected to arrive next spring. Gulnora says that the best part of her job is hearing children say goodbye to Nuri at the door.

items.prompt: Why did Sevara shop online?
items.answer: The nearest big shopping centre was far away
items.passage:
Last November, Sevara Yusupova decided to buy a winter coat for her mother's birthday. She was living in Namangan then, and the nearest big shopping centre was a two-hour bus ride away. Her friend suggested that she try an online store, and Sevara, who had never ordered anything over the internet before, felt a little nervous. She opened the website of a well-known company and began to browse.

There were more than four hundred coats in the women's section. Sevara used the filters to look only at warm coats in dark green, because her mother loved that colour. She read the descriptions carefully and spent almost an hour studying customers' reviews. One reviewer wrote that the sleeves were too short, so Sevara chose a larger size. In the end, she paid ninety-five thousand som, which included a discount of twenty percent.

The delivery was supposed to take three days, but the parcel did not arrive until the sixth day. Sevara was worried, and she wrote to the customer service team. A young man called Bobur answered within ten minutes. He told her that a snowstorm had closed the main road and that her parcel was now only fifty kilometres away. He also promised to refund the delivery fee, and he kept his promise the next morning.

When the coat finally came, Sevara opened the box with excitement, but her smile quickly disappeared. The colour was not dark green but light grey. She had been warned by her friend that this could happen, so she did not panic. She photographed the coat, filled in a return form and left the box at the post office. A week later, the correct coat arrived, and this time it fitted perfectly.

Sevara now says that online shopping is a good idea if people are careful. She advises beginners to read the return policy before paying, to check the reviews and never to use public wifi when entering bank details. Her mother wore the coat to the party on Saturday and received many compliments. Sevara has already ordered a pair of boots for herself, and she hopes they will come in the right colour.
options: The nearest big shopping centre was far away

items.prompt: Where did the rocket take off?
items.passage:
In the early hours of a cold morning in September, a rocket rose slowly from a launch site in Kazakhstan. On board were three astronauts, one from Russia, one from Italy and one from Canada, who were beginning a six-month mission to the International Space Station. Millions of people around the world watched the launch on their screens, and many schools in Uzbekistan arranged special lessons so that children could follow it live.

The journey to the station took only six hours, which was much shorter than the old two-day flights. When the spacecraft finally connected with the station, the crew had to wait for two hours while engineers checked that the doors were safe. Italian astronaut Chiara Ferrari later said that those two hours had felt like a whole day, because she had been dreaming about this moment since she was a little girl.

Life in space is very different from life on Earth. Because there is almost no gravity, the astronauts float rather than walk, and they sleep in bags fixed to the wall. They exercise for two hours every day to protect their muscles and bones, which become weaker in space. Food is also unusual. Water is recycled, even the water from the astronauts' sweat, and fresh fruit is a rare treat that arrives only with new supply ships.

The main purpose of the mission was science. The crew carried out forty-two experiments, including a study of how plants grow without soil. One experiment tested a new kind of glass that might be used in future telescopes. Another examined whether certain medicines work in the same way in space. The scientists on Earth hope that the results will help doctors treat patients and will also help farmers grow food in difficult places.

The astronauts returned to Earth in March, landing in a flat field near the city of Dzhezkazgan. After such a long time without gravity, they could not stand up on their own and had to be carried to a medical tent. Within a week, however, they were walking normally. Chiara said that the first thing she did at home was to drink a glass of cold water and listen to the rain.

items.prompt: What was Jasur's first popular video about?
items.passage:
Sixteen-year-old Jasur Normatov never expected that a short video about his grandmother's cooking would change his life. He had filmed it with an old phone in the kitchen of their house in Khiva, intending to show it only to his cousins. His grandmother was making traditional bread, and she talked to the camera as though she were telling a story to a child. Within a week, more than two hundred thousand people had watched the video.

Suddenly, Jasur had hundreds of messages every day. Some people asked for recipes, others wanted to visit Khiva, and a few offered him money to advertise their products. His parents were surprised, and a little worried. His father, who works as a teacher, told him that popularity could disappear as quickly as it arrived. They agreed on a rule: Jasur could continue making videos, but only after finishing his homework.

Jasur learned that making a good video was much harder than it looked. He spent four hours filming and about eight hours editing a single ten-minute episode. He taught himself to use free editing software and bought a cheap microphone after reading that bad sound was the main reason viewers stopped watching. He also learned to be careful. When a company offered him a large sum to say that a medicine was perfect, he refused, because he had not tried it himself.

By the end of the year, his channel had almost a million followers. Jasur used the money he earned to buy a better camera, but he also donated a part of it to the village school near Khiva, which needed new computers. He says that the best feeling in the world is receiving a letter from a stranger who cooked his grandmother's bread and enjoyed it.

Not everyone is positive, of course. Some people write unkind comments, and Jasur admits that they used to ruin his day. His grandmother gave him some useful advice: "If a person does not like the bread, you do not stop baking." Now he reads the comments only once a week. He plans to study film at university, but he says that he will never stop visiting his grandmother's kitchen.

items.prompt: What did the email say?
items.answer: His account would be closed in twenty-four hours
items.passage:
On a Tuesday evening in October, Rustam Ergashev, a bank clerk from Andijan, received an email that seemed to come from his favourite online music service. The message said that his account would be closed in twenty-four hours unless he confirmed his password. Rustam was tired after a long day, and he clicked on the link without thinking. The page looked exactly like the real website, so he typed in his details.

The next morning, he discovered that he could not enter his account. His password had been changed, and someone had bought three expensive gift cards using his bank card. Rustam felt sick. He called the bank at once, and an employee named Zarina helped him to block the card. Fortunately, the bank returned most of the money, because Rustam had reported the problem so quickly.

Later, a computer expert explained what had happened. The email was an example of phishing, a trick in which criminals pretend to be a trusted company in order to steal information. The expert, Anvar, pointed out that Rustam could have noticed several warning signs. The sender's address contained a spelling mistake, the message used strange language, and the link led to a web address that was slightly different from the original.

Anvar gave Rustam a list of simple rules. First, never click on links in emails that ask for personal information. Instead, open the website yourself and log in. Second, use a different password for every important account, and make each one at least twelve characters long. Third, turn on two-step verification, which sends a code to your phone every time someone tries to enter your account. If Rustam had used this system, the criminals would not have succeeded.

Rustam followed all of the advice, and he now uses a program that stores his passwords safely. He has also talked to his colleagues and to his elderly parents about the danger. His mother, who had once received a similar message, admitted that she had almost answered it. Rustam says that the experience was unpleasant, but it taught him that a few minutes of caution can save weeks of trouble.

items.prompt: How many electric cars are there in Tashkent today?
items.passage:
Ten years ago, an electric car was a rare sight on the streets of Tashkent. Today, the city has more than twelve thousand of them, and the number is growing every month. The government has reduced taxes on electric vehicles, and new charging stations have appeared near shopping centres, hotels and petrol stations. Many drivers say that they will never return to a petrol engine.

One of them is Otabek Rahimov, a taxi driver who bought his first electric car two years ago. He had been spending about forty percent of his income on fuel, and he was tired of the noise and smell of the old engine. After the change, he found that his monthly costs dropped by almost half. Electricity is cheaper than petrol, and the car needs fewer repairs, because it has fewer moving parts.

Of course, electric cars have problems too. The biggest worry is distance. Otabek's car can travel about three hundred kilometres on a full battery, but in cold winter weather the figure falls to about two hundred and twenty. He has learned to plan his day carefully and to charge the car during his lunch break. A fast charger can fill eighty percent of the battery in thirty minutes, but a slow charger at home needs the whole night.

Engineers are working on new batteries that would solve these difficulties. A factory near Jizzakh will begin producing batteries next year, and its managers claim that they will last for ten years. Scientists are also testing roads that charge cars while they are driving, although this technology is still very expensive. Some experts doubt that it will ever be widely used.

Critics point out that electric cars are only clean if the electricity itself is produced in a clean way. At present, much of the power in the country comes from natural gas, but new solar farms in the desert are changing this slowly. Otabek is hopeful. He says that when he started driving, the air in the city centre made his eyes hurt. Now, after a rainy morning, he can sometimes smell flowers from the park.

items.prompt: How many artists worked on the cartoon?
items.passage:
Making an animated film is a slow and patient job. In a small studio in Tashkent, a team of twenty-three artists spent almost three years creating a twelve-minute cartoon about a fox who wants to learn how to fly. The director, Shahlo Mirzaeva, says that when she first suggested the story, nobody believed that it could be finished. The studio had very little money, and most of the artists were young and inexperienced.

The process began with a script and hundreds of drawings. These pictures, called a storyboard, show every scene in the order in which it will appear. Shahlo drew the first version of the storyboard herself, working at her kitchen table in the evenings. Then the team discussed each scene. Sometimes they changed the ending completely; in the first version, the fox actually succeeded in flying, but they decided that it was more touching if he only learned to jump very high.

Next came the animation. For every second of film, the artists need to create twenty-four separate pictures. This means that the twelve-minute cartoon contained more than seventeen thousand images. Computers helped with the colours and the backgrounds, but the movements of the fox were drawn by hand. A young animator named Sardor said that he practised the fox's walk for a month, watching real foxes in a video from a nature programme.

Sound was another challenge. The voices were recorded by children from a local school, because the director wanted the characters to sound natural. The music was written by a violinist, and the sound of the wind was created by a student blowing across the top of a bottle. When the team added the sound to the pictures, they all agreed that the film suddenly seemed alive.

The cartoon was shown for the first time at a festival in Samarkand last spring, where it won a prize for the best short film by a new studio. Afterwards, an international television company bought it, and it has been translated into six languages. Shahlo says that the success was a surprise, but the most precious moment was watching a small girl in the cinema who cried when the fox fell and clapped when he got up.

items.prompt: Which school is the article about?
items.passage:
When the new artificial intelligence programs became popular, the teachers at School Number Twelve in Fergana were not sure what to do. Some of them wanted to forbid the programs completely. Others said that students would use them anyway, so it would be better to teach them how to use the tools sensibly. After a long meeting in September, the headmaster, Mr. Ismoilov, announced a compromise.

The new rule was simple. Students could ask the programs for explanations and examples, but they were not allowed to copy answers into their homework. Every student also had to write a short note describing how they had used the program. Mr. Ismoilov explained that the aim was honesty, not punishment. If a pupil had asked the machine to explain a difficult grammar rule, that was perfectly acceptable.

The English teacher, Ms. Kamola Aripova, was surprised by the results. She had expected that her students would become lazy, but the opposite happened. One of her pupils, Madina, asked the program to explain the difference between the past simple and the present perfect and then wrote her own examples. When Ms. Kamola checked them, she found only two mistakes. Madina said that the program had been patient and never got angry, even when she asked the same question four times.

However, the teachers also noticed some problems. The programs sometimes gave wrong information with great confidence. In a history lesson, one student wrote that a famous scientist had been born in the wrong century, because the machine had made a mistake. After this, Ms. Kamola taught her classes a new habit: always check important facts in a book or on a trusted website.

By December, most teachers agreed that the experiment had been a success. Test results had improved slightly, and fewer students had copied from each other. Mr. Ismoilov plans to organise a workshop for parents next month, where they can learn how the programs work. He believes that technology will not replace teachers, but teachers who understand technology may replace those who do not.

When the new artificial intelligence programs became popular, the teachers at School Number Twelve in Fergana were not sure what to do. Some of them wanted to forbid the programs completely. Others said that students would use them anyway, so it would be better to teach them how to use the tools sensibly. After a long meeting in September, the headmaster, Mr. Ismoilov, announced a compromise.

The new rule was simple. Students could ask the programs for explanations and examples, but they were not allowed to copy answers into their homework. Every student also had to write a short note describing how they had used the program. Mr. Ismoilov explained that the aim was honesty, not punishment. If a pupil had asked the machine to explain a difficult grammar rule, that was perfectly acceptable.

The English teacher, Ms. Kamola Aripova, was surprised by the results. She had expected that her students would become lazy, but the opposite happened. One of her pupils, Madina, asked the program to explain the difference between the past simple and the present perfect and then wrote her own examples. When Ms. Kamola checked them, she found only two mistakes. Madina said that the program had been patient and never got angry, even when she asked the same question four times.

However, the teachers also noticed some problems. The programs sometimes gave wrong information with great confidence. In a history lesson, one student wrote that a famous scientist had been born in the wrong century, because the machine had made a mistake. After this, Ms. Kamola taught her classes a new habit: always check important facts in a book or on a trusted website.

By December, most teachers agreed that the experiment had been a success. Test results had improved slightly, and fewer students had copied from each other. Mr. Ismoilov plans to organise a workshop for parents next month, where they can learn how the programs work. He believes that technology will not replace teachers, but teachers who understand technology may replace those who do not.

items.prompt: How far is the station from Tashkent?
items.passage:
High in the Chimgan mountains, about eighty kilometres from Tashkent, there is a small white building with a large antenna on its roof. This is a weather research station, and it has been collecting information about the climate for more than sixty years. Five scientists work there throughout the year, and in winter they sometimes cannot leave for weeks because the road is covered with snow.

The head of the station, Dr. Nilufar Hamidova, begins every day at six o'clock. First, she reads the numbers from the instruments outside: temperature, wind speed, humidity and the amount of snow on the ground. These measurements are sent by computer to the national weather service, which uses them to make forecasts for the whole country. If the data are wrong, the forecasts will be wrong as well, so she checks every instrument twice.

In recent years, the scientists have noticed worrying changes. The glaciers near the station are melting faster than before. A photograph taken in 1985 shows a thick river of ice reaching almost to the valley, while today the ice ends nearly two kilometres higher. Because many farmers in the region depend on water from melting snow, this change could cause serious problems in the future.

The station also uses satellites. A satellite can photograph huge areas of land in a single day and can measure the thickness of clouds. Dr. Nilufar explained that the satellite pictures are most useful when they are compared with measurements from the ground. "The satellite sees the whole forest," she says, "but we can touch the trees." Together, the two methods give a much clearer picture of what is happening.

The work is not always comfortable. The station has no shop, the nearest village is a two-hour walk away, and the internet connection often fails during storms. However, the scientists say they would not change their jobs. Last summer, a group of schoolchildren visited the station, and Dr. Nilufar showed them how to launch a weather balloon. When it reached the clouds, one boy shouted that he wanted to become a scientist too.

Today, however, professional gaming, known as esports, has become a serious sport with big prizes and millions of fans. Last year, the final of an international tournament in Seoul attracted more than forty thousand spectators in the stadium and several million more online.

One of the rising stars of the Uzbek esports scene is Sherzod Tursunov, a twenty-year-old player from Qarshi. He started playing strategy games at the age of eleven, in an internet cafe near his home. At first, his father was against it, and Sherzod had to hide his hobby. The situation changed when he won a regional competition and received a prize of five million som. His father, who had been a football player in his youth, finally understood that talent can appear in many forms.

Life as a professional player is not as easy as it looks. Sherzod's team trains for eight hours every day, six days a week. They analyse recordings of their games, discuss mistakes and practise new tactics. The coach, a former player named Ilhom, insists that they also do physical exercise, because sitting for long hours without moving can damage the back and wrists. Every morning begins with a thirty-minute run.

The team also pays attention to health and sleep. Ilhom has forbidden energy drinks and late-night snacks, and he asks the players to be in bed by midnight. He says that concentration is more important than speed. "A tired player makes silly mistakes," he often repeats. In a recent tournament, the team lost a match because one player had slept for only three hours the night before.

Sherzod knows that a career in esports is short, because players usually retire at around twenty-six. For this reason, he is studying computer science by distance learning. He hopes to become a game designer one day. Meanwhile, his team is preparing for the national championship in Tashkent in March, and they believe that this year they have a real chance of winning the first place.

items.prompt: In which town do the friends record the podcast?
items.passage:
In a quiet street in Nukus, in a room above a bakery, two friends record a podcast every Friday evening. The programme is called Voices of the Aral, and it tells stories about the people who live near the old sea. Its creators, Aysulu and Daniyar, started it three years ago with a cheap microphone and a laptop that sometimes switched itself off in the middle of a recording.

The idea came from Aysulu's grandfather, who used to be a fisherman. As a child, she listened to his stories about enormous fish, dangerous storms and a harbour that was full of boats. When the sea disappeared, the stories seemed to disappear too. Aysulu realised that the older generation would not live for ever, and that somebody had to record their memories. She asked her friend Daniyar, who studied journalism, to help her.

The first episode was not a success. The sound was bad, the interview was too long, and only eleven people downloaded it. However, the friends did not give up. They watched videos about interviewing, practised speaking clearly and chose shorter topics. After six months, they had about three hundred listeners, and a local radio station offered them a short slot on Sunday mornings.

Today the podcast has more than twelve thousand listeners, many of them living abroad. One episode, about a woman who had saved her village's last boat, was heard by a famous writer, who invited the pair to a book festival in Tashkent. Daniyar says that the most important lesson was patience. "At the beginning, we thought that success would come in a week," he laughs. "It took three years."

The friends have also noticed that the podcast has changed the community. Young people have started to ask their grandparents questions, and several families have found old photographs to share. Next month, Aysulu and Daniyar will open a small exhibition in the town library. It will show those photographs together with a map of the old harbour and recordings of the voices, which visitors can hear through headphones.

items.prompt: How old is Bekzod?
items.passage:
Eleven-year-old Bekzod lost three fingers on his left hand in an accident with a farm machine when he was seven. For four years, he found it difficult to do ordinary things, like tying his shoes, opening a bottle or holding a pencil. A traditional artificial hand would have cost more than eight thousand dollars, and his family, who live in a village near Termez, could not afford it.

Then a volunteer from a university heard about his case. Dr. Ravshan Tojiev leads a small group of engineers who make artificial hands with a 3D printer. The machine builds objects slowly, layer by layer, from plastic. Each hand costs only about fifty dollars for the materials, and the design is available free on the internet. The team has already made nineteen hands for children in different parts of the country.

Making Bekzod's hand took three weeks. First, the engineers measured his arm and took photographs from different angles. They used a computer program to adjust the design so that the hand would fit comfortably. The printing itself lasted about thirty hours, and then the parts were joined with small strings and screws. When Bekzod moves his wrist, the fingers close, and he can hold light objects.

The first day with the new hand was emotional. Bekzod picked up a glass of water by himself and drank from it, and his mother started to cry. Later, he tried to catch a ball, which was much harder, and he dropped it nine times. However, he laughed every time. The engineers chose a bright orange colour because Bekzod said that he wanted a hand that looked like a robot's.

Because children grow quickly, the hands have to be replaced about once a year, and this is one reason why 3D printing is so useful. A new, larger hand can be produced in a few days at a low price. Dr. Ravshan hopes to open a workshop in every region of the country. He says that the technology is not magic, but it gives children something precious: the chance to play like everyone else.

items.prompt: When was the online encyclopedia founded?
items.passage:
Many students use the online encyclopedia every day, but few of them know how it is written. Unlike a traditional encyclopedia, which is produced by a small group of experts and printed in heavy volumes, this one is created by volunteers. Anyone with an internet connection can add information, correct a mistake or improve an explanation. The site was founded in 2001, and today it contains articles in more than three hundred languages.

One of the volunteers is Laylo Abdullaeva, a retired librarian from Margilan. She began to edit articles six years ago after she noticed that the page about her town was very short and contained several errors. Laylo spent two weeks in the local archive, reading old newspapers and books about the history of silk production. Then she wrote a new article of three thousand words, with photographs and a list of sources.

According to the rules of the site, every statement must be supported by a reliable source. If an editor writes that a bridge was opened in 1950, he or she must show a book or newspaper which says the same. Other volunteers check the new articles, and if there is no evidence, they remove the sentence. Laylo says that this system is not perfect, but that it works better than most people expect.

Vandalism is a problem, however. Sometimes people add silly or false information just for fun. Special programs help to find such changes, and experienced volunteers can restore the old version within minutes. Laylo remembers an occasion when someone changed the page about her town to say that it had a population of ten million. It was corrected in less than four minutes.

Teachers have mixed opinions about the encyclopedia. Some say that students should never use it, because anybody can change it. Others, like Laylo, think that it is a good place to begin research, as long as students follow the links to the original sources. She often visits schools and teaches children how to edit articles. In her opinion, the best way to understand how knowledge works is to take part in making it.

items.prompt: Which region is the article about?
items.passage:
Farmers in the Kashkadarya region have always depended on the weather, but recently a new helper has appeared in their fields. It flies, it makes a soft buzzing sound, and it carries a camera. The helper is a drone, and it is changing the way people grow cotton and wheat. Many farmers were doubtful at first, but the results have convinced even the most traditional ones.

Bahrom Qodirov, who owns sixty hectares of land near Shahrisabz, bought his first drone two seasons ago. Before that, he used to walk around the fields every morning to look for problems, and this took him nearly four hours. Now the drone covers the same area in twenty minutes. The pictures show him which parts of the field are too dry, which plants are sick and where insects have appeared.

The drone does not only take pictures. A special program studies the colours of the leaves and creates a map in which healthy areas are green and weak areas are red. Using this map, Bahrom waters only the places that need water. In the first year, he reduced his water use by about a quarter. In a region where water is scarce, this is an enormous advantage.

Some larger drones can also spread fertiliser or protect plants from insects. They fly low above the field and release exactly the right amount of liquid. Experts say that this method uses fewer chemicals than a tractor, which covers the whole ground. It is also safer for workers, because nobody needs to stand in a cloud of spray.

However, drones are not cheap. A good model costs about three thousand dollars, and training is necessary. To help small farms, the regional government has organised a shared service, in which several farmers pay together for a pilot and a machine. Bahrom is the head of one such group. He says that his father laughed at the idea of a flying machine in a field, but last harvest, the old man asked for a flight to see his favourite apple tree from above.

items.prompt: How long had it been raining before the flood?
items.passage:
Last spring, the village of Qo'shrabot near Samarkand experienced the worst flood in forty years. Dilnoza Rahimova, a schoolteacher who has lived there all her life, remembers the night very clearly. It had been raining heavily for three days, and by Thursday evening the small river behind the school had risen almost two metres above its normal level.

At around nine o'clock, the village leader, Mr Karimov, rang the old bell outside the mosque to warn everyone. Dilnoza had already packed a bag with documents, medicine and some bread, because her neighbour had told her that the water might reach the main road by midnight. If she had ignored the warning, she would probably have been trapped in her house. Instead, she walked with her two children to the school, which stands on higher ground and was used as a shelter.

By ten o'clock, about one hundred and twenty people had arrived. The volunteers had put mattresses in the classrooms, and the cook from the local cafe made hot soup for everyone. Dilnoza said that the children were frightened at first, but a young volunteer named Jasur played games with them until they fell asleep. Outside, the water continued to rise, and several cars were carried away along the street.

The flood reached its highest point at four o'clock in the morning. Forty-three houses were damaged, and two bridges were destroyed. Fortunately, nobody was seriously hurt, because the villagers had been warned in time. The next day, soldiers arrived with boats and helped to rescue three families who had stayed in their homes on the lower streets.

It took the community almost two months to clean the streets and repair the damage. Farmers lost many of their vegetables, and the government promised to pay part of the cost. items.prompt: Who suggested starting the recycling project?
items.passage:
Two years ago, our school in Tashkent had a serious rubbish problem. Every day, students threw away hundreds of plastic bottles, paper cups and sheets of paper. The head teacher, Mrs Yusupova, said that if nothing changed, the school would soon produce more waste than it could handle. That was the moment when a group of students decided to start a recycling project.

The idea came from a fifteen-year-old girl called Madina. She had read an article about a school in Germany where students sorted their rubbish into five different bins. Madina asked her friends whether they could do the same thing, and within a week twenty students had joined her club. They called it the Green Team.

First, the team bought coloured bins with money that was collected at a school fair. Blue bins were for paper, yellow bins for plastic, green bins for glass, and a large grey bin for everything else. Each classroom received a set of small bins, and Madina made posters that explained which items belonged where. At the beginning, many students were confused, and the cleaners often found banana skins in the plastic bin.

After one month, the situation improved. The Green Team checked the bins every Friday and gave a small prize to the class that had sorted its rubbish best. The winners received a plant for their classroom. Students became very competitive, and some classes even reminded their teachers to use the correct bins.

The results were impressive. In the first year, the school recycled almost eight tonnes of paper and nearly two tonnes of plastic. A local company collected the materials every two weeks and paid the school a small amount of money. The school used this money to buy new books for the library.

Madina says that the most difficult part was changing people's habits. Some teachers thought that the project would be too much work, but they changed their minds when they saw how enthusiastic the students were. Next year, the Green Team plans to build a compost area in the school garden so that food waste can be turned into soil.

Mrs Yusupova is very proud of the students. She believes that the project has taught them that small actions can make a big difference, and she hopes that other schools in the city will follow their example.

items.prompt: What does Uncle Bobur do at the park?
items.passage:
Last Saturday, my family visited the Chorvoq Wildlife Park, which is about ninety kilometres from Tashkent. My uncle Bobur works there as a guide, and he had invited us to spend the day with him. We left home at six o'clock in the morning, and we arrived just before the park opened at eight.

Our first stop was the bird house, where we saw more than fifty species. My little sister Zarina was delighted by a bright green parrot that could say "hello" in three languages. Uncle Bobur explained that many of the birds had been injured and were being cared for until they could return to the wild. A vet named Dr Aliyeva told us that she treats about two hundred animals every year.

After that, we walked through the forest trail, where we hoped to see deer. We waited quietly for twenty minutes, and finally a mother deer appeared with her baby. Uncle Bobur whispered that the park has twelve deer, and that they are very shy. He also told us that visitors must never feed the animals, because human food can make them sick.

At noon, we had lunch beside a small lake. A group of ducks swam close to our table, and Zarina threw a few pieces of bread to them. Immediately, a ranger came and politely reminded her about the rules. She felt embarrassed, but my uncle laughed and said that almost every child makes the same mistake.

The highlight of the day was the afternoon talk about wolves. The park rescued two young wolves five years ago after hunters had destroyed their home. Now they live in a large area of the forest, and visitors can watch them from a special wooden tower. A ranger explained that wolves are not dangerous to people if they are left alone, and that they are very important for keeping nature in balance.

We left the park at five o'clock, tired but happy. Before we went home, I bought a small book about local animals in the gift shop, and the money from the shop goes directly to the animal hospital. I would love to return in autumn, when the leaves change colour and the park is supposed to be even more beautiful.

items.prompt: Why did the friends not take heavy coats?
items.passage:
On a cold Sunday in February, four friends set out to climb a mountain in the Chimgan hills, east of Tashkent. The weather forecast had said that the day would be sunny, so they did not take heavy coats or extra food. By two o'clock in the afternoon, however, the sky had turned dark, and thick snow began to fall.

The group leader, a twenty-two-year-old student named Sardor, realised that they had lost the path. His phone had only ten percent of its battery left, but he managed to call the emergency number and explained where they thought they were. Then he switched the phone off to save power, and the four friends sat together behind a large rock to protect themselves from the wind.

The mountain rescue team received the call at two forty. Its leader, Captain Orifov, immediately sent six rescuers with a dog named Rex, who had been trained to find people in snow. The rescuers drove as far as the road allowed, and then they walked for almost three hours through deep snow. Because it was getting dark, they carried bright lamps and hot tea.

At around six o'clock, Rex began to bark and ran towards the rock. The friends were cold and frightened, but none of them was injured. One of them, a girl called Nargiza, had started to feel very sleepy, which Captain Orifov said is a dangerous sign of extreme cold. The rescuers gave her a blanket and warm drinks, and they checked everyone carefully before starting the walk back.

The group reached the road at nine o'clock that evening, where an ambulance was waiting. All four were taken to hospital for a check, and they were allowed to go home the following morning.

Afterwards, Captain Orifov gave some advice to people who enjoy hiking. He said that nobody should trust the weather forecast completely, and that every hiker must carry warm clothes, water, food and a fully charged phone. He also added that it is wise to tell a friend or family member where you are going and when you plan to return.

Sardor admitted that the group had made several mistakes. He promised that next time they would prepare much more carefully, and he thanked the rescue team for saving their lives.

items.prompt: How much rain fell between May and August?
items.passage:
In the summer of last year, the Khorezm region suffered one of the longest droughts in its recent history. From the beginning of May until the end of August, only eleven millimetres of rain fell, which is less than a tenth of the usual amount. Temperatures were also extremely high, and on the hottest day the thermometer showed forty-six degrees.

Farmers were the first to feel the problem. Rustam Qodirov, who grows cotton and melons near the town of Urgench, said that his fields looked like a desert by July. The canals which normally bring water from the Amu Darya river were almost empty, and he could only water his land twice a month instead of every week. In the end, he lost nearly half of his melon harvest.

The drought affected ordinary families, too. In many villages, the wells dried up, and tankers had to bring drinking water from the city. The government introduced new rules, so that people were not allowed to wash their cars or water their gardens during the daytime. Some households received water for only four hours a day.

Animals suffered as well. Shepherds had to take their sheep much farther to find grass, and several of them sold part of their flocks because they could not afford food for them. Wild birds came into the towns, searching for water in gardens and fountains. Local children put out small bowls of water for them, and a teacher in Khiva organised a campaign to protect the storks.

In September, the first rain finally arrived. It was gentle at first, but then it became a heavy storm that lasted two days. People stood in the streets and laughed, and many of them said that they had never been so happy to get wet.

Experts from the university say that droughts like this may become more common in the future. They recommend that farmers use drip irrigation, which saves up to half of the water, and that cities repair old pipes, because almost a quarter of the water is lost through leaks. Rustam has already decided to follow their advice, and he plans to install the new system before next spring.

items.prompt: Where does the saiga antelope live?
items.passage:
The saiga antelope is a strange-looking animal with a large, soft nose and thin legs. It lives on the open steppes of Central Asia, including the northern part of Uzbekistan, the Ustyurt plateau. Thirty years ago, there were hundreds of thousands of saigas, but hunting reduced their numbers so quickly that by the year two thousand only a few thousand remained.

Dr Gulnora Ismoilova is a biologist who has studied the saiga for fifteen years. She explains that the animals were hunted mainly for their horns, which were sold for traditional medicine. Another problem was that roads and fences blocked the routes that saigas follow when they travel in search of food. Without enough grass, the mothers were too weak to feed their young.

In two thousand and eleven, a conservation project started in the region. It was supported by local authorities and by an international organisation. First, new laws were introduced to protect the animals, and rangers were employed to patrol the steppe. Next, some of the fences were removed, so that the herds could travel freely. Finally, the team began to teach villagers about the importance of saigas and offered them jobs as guides for visitors.

The results have been encouraging. According to the latest count, there are now about two thousand five hundred saigas on the Ustyurt plateau, which is nearly five times as many as there were ten years ago. Dr Ismoilova says that the number would have been even higher if a disease had not killed thousands of saigas in Kazakhstan a few years ago. That event showed scientists how fragile the population still is.

The team uses small cameras and satellite collars to follow the herds. In spring, they watch the females carefully, because all the babies are born within the same two weeks. During that time, visitors are not allowed near the calving areas.

Dr Ismoilova is hopeful but careful. She believes that the saiga can survive if people continue to protect the steppe, and she hopes that her own daughter will one day see a herd of ten thousand animals running across the plateau.
