title: O'qish 23
intro: Har bir matnni diqqat bilan o'qing va uning savollariga javob bering.

items.prompt: How long did the grey cloud cover Navoi?
items.passage:
Nobody in Navoi can forget the winter of two years ago, when a thick grey cloud covered the city for almost two weeks. Cold air stayed close to the ground, and smoke from factories and cars could not escape. On the worst day, the air quality index reached two hundred and sixty, which is considered dangerous for everybody.

Malika Hasanova, a doctor at the city hospital, said that the number of patients with breathing problems doubled during that period. Many of them were children and elderly people. She remembers an old man who had never had asthma before but who had to spend four nights in the hospital. Malika advised families to stay indoors, to keep their windows closed and to wear masks whenever they went out.

The city council reacted quickly. For ten days, heavy trucks were forbidden to enter the centre, and two factories were asked to reduce production. Schools were closed for three days, and the children studied at home using online lessons. The mayor also announced that the buses would be free, so that fewer people would use their own cars.

In the following months, the authorities made some long-term decisions. They planted more than five thousand trees along the main roads, because trees absorb dust and harmful gases. They also agreed with the factory owners that new filters would be installed on all chimneys by the end of the next year. In addition, a new network of sensors was placed around the city, and the results can now be checked on a mobile app.

Some citizens decided to help, too. A group of students from the technical college started a campaign called "Leave the Car at Home", and about eight hundred families promised to use bicycles or public transport at least twice a week. The organisers say that it is a small change but that it is already visible in the traffic.

Last winter, the air quality index never went above one hundred and twenty. Malika is pleased, but she warns that the problem has not disappeared. She says that clean air should not be a luxury, and that everybody has a duty to protect it.

Cold air stayed close to the ground, and smoke from factories and cars could not escape. On the worst day, the air quality index reached two hundred and sixty, which is considered dangerous for everybody.

Malika Hasanova, a doctor at the city hospital, said that the number of patients with breathing problems doubled during that period. Many of them were children and elderly people. She remembers an old man who had never had asthma before but who had to spend four nights in the hospital. Malika advised families to stay indoors, to keep their windows closed and to wear masks whenever they went out.

The city council reacted quickly. For ten days, heavy trucks were forbidden to enter the centre, and two factories were asked to reduce production. Schools were closed for three days, and the children studied at home using online lessons. The mayor also announced that the buses would be free, so that fewer people would use their own cars.

In the following months, the authorities made some long-term decisions. They planted more than five thousand trees along the main roads, because trees absorb dust and harmful gases. They also agreed with the factory owners that new filters would be installed on all chimneys by the end of the next year. In addition, a new network of sensors was placed around the city, and the results can now be checked on a mobile app.

Some citizens decided to help, too. A group of students from the technical college started a campaign called "Leave the Car at Home", and about eight hundred families promised to use bicycles or public transport at least twice a week. The organisers say that it is a small change but that it is already visible in the traffic.

Last winter, the air quality index never went above one hundred and twenty. Malika is pleased, but she warns that the problem has not disappeared. She says that clean air should not be a luxury, and that everybody has a duty to protect it.

items.prompt: Where did Timur go on holiday?
items.passage:
Dear Ibrohim,

Greetings from the coast of Norway! I have been here for five days now, and I have so much to tell you. When I first decided to go on a whale watching trip, I was worried that I would be disappointed. A friend of mine had once travelled for hours on a boat and had not seen a single whale. This time, however, I was extremely lucky.

We left the small harbour of Andenes at nine o'clock on Tuesday morning. There were thirty passengers on the boat, and the weather was cold but dry. Our guide, a cheerful woman named Ingrid, told us that the sea here is very deep, and that sperm whales come close to the shore to hunt for squid. She said that we would probably need to wait for about an hour before we could see anything.

In fact, we spotted the first whale after only forty minutes. It appeared suddenly, about two hundred metres from the boat, and blew a high cloud of water into the air. Everyone shouted and took photographs. Ingrid said that the animal was a male, almost sixteen metres long, and that it would stay underwater for about forty-five minutes before coming back to breathe.

We followed him for two hours. Later, we also saw a group of dolphins which jumped beside the boat, and a few seals resting on the rocks. A little boy named Lars was so excited that he nearly fell into the water, and his father held him by the jacket!

I learned many interesting facts during the trip. For example, whales sleep with only half of their brain at a time, so that they can continue breathing. Ingrid also explained that the company follows strict rules: the boats must stay at least one hundred metres from the animals, and they must switch off the engines when whales are near.

The trip cost me eighty euros, which I think is a fair price. I took more than three hundred photos, and I cannot wait to show them to you. If you have the chance, you must come here next summer. I promise that you will never forget it.

Your friend,
Timur

items.prompt: When did the storm hit Termez?
items.passage:
On the night of the fourteenth of October, a powerful storm hit the town of Termez. The wind blew at nearly one hundred and thirty kilometres per hour, and the rain fell so heavily that the streets turned into rivers within minutes. Although the weather service had warned people two days earlier, few of them believed that the storm would be so serious.

My grandfather, Abdulla, was sleeping when the noise woke him up. He looked out of the window and saw a large tree fall onto the neighbour's garage. Then the electricity went out, and the whole street became completely dark. He told us afterwards that he had never been so frightened in his seventy years. He took a torch, woke my grandmother, and they both went down to the cellar, which he had always thought was unnecessary.

The storm lasted for about three hours. By morning, more than two hundred roofs had been damaged, and about a thousand trees had been broken or pulled out of the ground. The market had lost its tin roof, and the old bridge near the station was covered with branches. Telephone lines were cut, and for two days the town had no electricity.

What I remember most clearly is the way people behaved. As soon as the wind stopped, neighbours came out with ladders, saws and buckets. A group of teenagers cut up the fallen trees and carried the wood to elderly people for their stoves. A baker opened his shop and gave bread to anyone who needed it, without asking for money. My grandfather said that the town had never been so united.

It took the electricity company four days to repair the main cables. In the meantime, the school served as a centre where residents could charge their phones and get hot food. The mayor visited the area and promised that the town would plant two thousand new trees in the spring.

Since that night, my grandfather has kept an emergency box in his cellar, which contains candles, matches, water and a small radio. He often says that nature teaches us humility, and that a person who listens to a warning is never foolish.

items.prompt: What fell onto the neighbour's garage?
items.passage:
On the night of the fourteenth of October, a powerful storm hit the town of Termez. The wind blew at nearly one hundred and thirty kilometres per hour, and the rain fell so heavily that the streets turned into rivers within minutes. Although the weather service had warned people two days earlier, few of them believed that the storm would be so serious.

My grandfather, Abdulla, was sleeping when the noise woke him up. He looked out of the window and saw a large tree fall onto the neighbour's garage. Then the electricity went out, and the whole street became completely dark. He told us afterwards that he had never been so frightened in his seventy years. He took a torch, woke my grandmother, and they both went down to the cellar, which he had always thought was unnecessary.

The storm lasted for about three hours. By morning, more than two hundred roofs had been damaged, and about a thousand trees had been broken or pulled out of the ground. The market had lost its tin roof, and the old bridge near the station was covered with branches. Telephone lines were cut, and for two days the town had no electricity.

What I remember most clearly is the way people behaved. As soon as the wind stopped, neighbours came out with ladders, saws and buckets. A group of teenagers cut up the fallen trees and carried the wood to elderly people for their stoves. A baker opened his shop and gave bread to anyone who needed it, without asking for money. My grandfather said that the town had never been so united.

It took the electricity company four days to repair the main cables. In the meantime, the school served as a centre where residents could charge their phones and get hot food. The mayor visited the area and promised that the town would plant two thousand new trees in the spring.

Since that night, my grandfather has kept an emergency box in his cellar, which contains candles, matches, water and a small radio. He often says that nature teaches us humility, and that a person who listens to a warning is never foolish.

items.prompt: How many hives does Bobomurod keep?
items.passage:
Bobomurod Aliyev has kept bees for thirty-five years in the hills near Shahrisabz. He keeps sixty hives on a hillside covered with wild flowers, and every summer he produces about one and a half tonnes of honey. When I visited his farm last June, he showed me around and explained why bees are so important for people.

Bobomurod began by telling me that one hive can contain up to fifty thousand bees, but only one of them is the queen. She lays about two thousand eggs every day and can live for five years. The workers, which are all female, live for only six weeks in summer. They clean the hive, feed the young, bring food and protect the colony from enemies. The male bees, called drones, do not work at all, and in autumn they are driven out of the hive.

Then he explained how honey is made. A worker bee visits hundreds of flowers and collects a sweet liquid called nectar. Back in the hive, she passes it to other bees, who dry it until it becomes thick. To make just one kilogram of honey, the bees have to fly a distance equal to going around the earth several times. When I heard that, I began to treat each spoonful with more respect.

Bobomurod then gave me a protective hat and led me to one of the hives. I was nervous, but he told me to move slowly and to stay calm. He used a small metal can of smoke, which makes the bees quiet, and lifted the lid. I could hear a soft humming sound, and I saw thousands of bees working on yellow combs.

My host also spoke about a serious problem. In the last ten years, he has lost almost a third of his bees because of chemicals used on nearby fields and because of changes in the weather. Some of the flowers now open earlier than before, and the bees are not ready. He believes that if bees disappeared, many fruits and vegetables would also disappear, because bees carry pollen from one plant to another.

Before I left, he gave me a jar of dark honey from the mountain flowers. It tasted better than anything I have ever bought in a shop. He smiled and said that it is a gift from his bees, not from him.

Some of the flowers now open earlier than before, and the bees are not ready. He believes that if bees disappeared, many fruits and vegetables would also disappear, because bees carry pollen from one plant to another.

items.prompt: How old were the participants of the camp?
items.passage:
Last August, I took part in a one-week climate camp in the Fergana Valley, and it was one of the most interesting experiences of my life. The camp was organised by a non-profit group and was open to young people between sixteen and twenty. There were forty participants from all over Uzbekistan, and I shared a tent with three girls from Nukus, Bukhara and Andijan.

Every morning began at seven o'clock with a short run, followed by breakfast made from local products. After that, we attended lectures given by scientists and engineers. On the first day, a professor from Fergana State University showed us graphs which proved that the average temperature in the region has risen by almost two degrees in the last fifty years. He said that this is the reason why glaciers in the mountains are melting faster, and that, if nothing is done, many rivers will be much smaller by the end of the century.

The afternoons were more practical. We learned how to build a simple solar cooker using a cardboard box and aluminium paper, and by Wednesday we were cooking eggs in the sun. On Thursday, an engineer taught us how to measure the energy used in a house. My team found that our tent's phone chargers used more electricity than we had expected, and we decided to share them.

The most memorable day was Friday, when we planted three hundred young trees on a hill near the village of Rishton. The local farmers had been waiting for volunteers for months, because the hill had lost most of its soil during heavy rains. It was hard work, and my hands were covered with blisters, but I was proud when I looked at the green line of trees at the end of the day.

On the last evening, each group presented a plan for its own school or neighbourhood. Mine suggested installing solar panels on the roof of our school gym. If the directors accept it, the school could save about twenty percent of its electricity bill.

I came back home with new friends and a clear idea of what I want to study. I am now planning to become an environmental engineer, and I have already started a small climate club at my school.

items.prompt: Where is the camel farm?
items.passage:
Few animals are better adapted to life in the desert than the camel. During a school trip last spring, our class visited a camel farm in the Kyzylkum Desert, about one hundred and fifty kilometres from Bukhara. The farm belongs to a family, and the owner, Mr Normatov, welcomed us with green tea and fresh bread.

He began with some surprising facts. A camel can drink up to one hundred litres of water in only ten minutes and then walk for several days without drinking again. Contrary to popular belief, the hump does not store water; it stores fat, which the animal uses as energy when food is difficult to find. The thick eyelashes and the narrow nose protect the camel from sand, and its wide feet prevent it from sinking into the ground.

Mr Normatov has one hundred and ten camels, and each of them has a name. He told us that his grandfather started the farm in nineteen fifty and that, at that time, camels were the only transport across the sand. Today, people use trucks and motorbikes, so the farm earns its money in different ways. It sells camel milk, which is believed to be very healthy, and wool, which is used for making warm blankets. In summer, the family also receives tourists who want to ride across the dunes.

We were allowed to take a short ride, and it was funnier than I expected. Camels stand up with their back legs first, so I almost fell forward. My friend Shahlo laughed so much that her camel, called Oqtosh, stopped and refused to walk for five minutes. The guide said that camels are very intelligent and that they can remember bad treatment for years.

Before we left, Mr Normatov showed us a small baby camel that had been born three days earlier. It could already stand up and walk beside its mother. He explained that calves must be protected from the cold at night, because the desert can be freezing even after a hot day.

On the way back, our teacher asked us to write a short report about the visit. I decided to write about the camel's special abilities, because I now believe that this animal deserves much more respect than most people give it.

items.prompt: What did Elyor find in his net one morning?
items.passage:
Aydarkul is a large lake in the middle of Uzbekistan, and every year thousands of visitors come to enjoy its blue water and quiet beaches. Unfortunately, the same visitors often leave a lot of rubbish behind them. Last September, a group of volunteers decided to do something about it.

The idea came from a young fisherman named Elyor Tursunov. One morning, he noticed that his net had caught more plastic bags than fish, and he decided that he could no longer ignore the problem. He published a short message on social media, asking for help, and he was surprised when more than three hundred people replied within two days.

The cleaning day was organised for the last Saturday of the month. People arrived by bus, car and even bicycle, and they were divided into small teams. Each team received gloves, strong bags and a map of the beach. Local shops donated drinking water and sandwiches, and a company lent two small boats for collecting rubbish from the water.

By two o'clock in the afternoon, the volunteers had filled almost nine hundred bags. They found bottles, tyres, broken chairs, fishing lines and even an old refrigerator. A teacher who joined the action with her students said that the most shocking discovery was a large pile of cigarette ends, which she estimated to be several thousand. She explained that each cigarette end can pollute up to fifty litres of water.

When the work was over, the group sat on the beach and had a picnic. Elyor thanked everyone and announced that a new sign would be placed at the entrance, asking visitors to take their rubbish home. He also said that the municipality had agreed to put twenty additional bins along the shore and to empty them twice a week.

Within a month, the beach looked completely different. Birds returned to the quiet corners of the lake, and the fishermen reported that their nets were cleaner. Elyor says that the main change must happen in people's heads, and that the volunteers have promised to repeat the event every season until the lake is clean for good.

items.prompt: How much of its water has the Aral Sea lost?
items.passage:
The Aral Sea was once the fourth largest lake in the world, but since the nineteen sixties it has lost more than ninety percent of its water. Rivers that used to flow into it were turned into canals to irrigate cotton fields, and the sea slowly shrank. Today, parts of its former bottom form a dry, salty desert called Aralkum.

Dr Farhod Nazarov is a scientist who has been working in this area for twelve years. I interviewed him last month, when he returned to Tashkent for a conference. He told me that the first time he saw the old harbour in Moynaq, he could not believe his eyes. Large rusty ships were standing in the sand, more than one hundred kilometres from the nearest water.

Dr Nazarov explained that the disappearance of the sea has had serious effects on local people. The climate has become hotter in summer and colder in winter, and strong winds carry salt and dust over great distances. Many families have left, because fishing, which had been their main job, is no longer possible. Health problems such as asthma and kidney disease are common among those who stayed.

However, he does not think that the situation is hopeless. In recent years, the government and international organisations have begun to plant a special desert tree called saxaul on the dry seabed. So far, more than a million hectares have been covered. The roots of these trees hold the soil in place and reduce the dust storms. In addition, a dam was built in Kazakhstan, which has helped the northern part of the sea to recover; fish have returned, and some fishermen have returned with them.

Dr Nazarov's own project is about finding crops that can grow in salty soil. His team has tested nine plants, and two of them have given good results. He hopes that local farmers will be able to use them soon, so that they can earn money without wasting water.

items.prompt: How long was Kamola away?
items.passage:
Last winter, my cousin Kamola, who is a marine biologist, joined an expedition to Antarctica. She was away for ninety days and sent us long messages whenever the satellite connection worked. Now that she has come home, she has shown us hundreds of photographs and told us many stories, but the ones about penguins are my favourites.

The expedition included twenty scientists from eight countries, and their mission was to count the emperor penguins living near the coast. Emperor penguins are the largest of all penguins; they can be up to one metre and ten centimetres tall. They spend the whole winter on the ice, where the temperature can fall to minus sixty degrees, and the wind can blow at two hundred kilometres per hour.

Kamola explained how these birds survive. The males gather in a large group, called a huddle, and stand very close together to keep warm. Each penguin takes a turn to stand on the outside, where it is coldest, and then moves slowly towards the middle. The mothers lay one egg and then travel to the sea to find food, which can take two months. During this period, the fathers keep the egg on their feet under a warm fold of skin, and they do not eat anything at all.

One day, Kamola nearly had an accident. She was walking on the ice with a colleague when the surface began to crack, and they had to run back to the camp. She laughed when she remembered it, but she admitted that she had been terrified. The team had been trained to move in pairs and to carry long poles to test the ice before each step.

As well as counting penguins, the scientists measured the size of the ice. Their results were worrying, because the ice is becoming thinner every year. If the ice melts too early, the chicks cannot grow strong enough to swim, and many of them die. Kamola believes that penguins may be one of the first animals to suffer from climate change.

She is now writing a report for a scientific journal, and she hopes that it will convince governments to protect the area. In the meantime, she has promised to give a talk at my school next month, and I am sure that everyone will want to hear about her adventure.

items.prompt: Why did Bell's family move to Canada?
items.answer: Because the doctors worried about his health
items.passage:
Alexander Graham Bell was born in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1847. His father and grandfather were both teachers of speech, so Alexander grew up surrounded by the study of sounds and voices. His mother gradually lost her hearing, and this experience made him determined to find better ways of helping people who could not hear. When he was twenty-three, his family moved to Canada because the doctors feared that the damp Scottish weather might damage his health.

A year later Bell moved to Boston, where he started to teach deaf children how to speak. He was a patient and enthusiastic teacher, and many parents were grateful to him. In the evenings, however, he worked on his own experiments. He believed that it was possible to send the human voice along a wire, just as telegraph machines already sent short electrical signals. Many of his friends laughed at the idea, but he refused to give up.

He could not do the work alone, so he hired a young electrician named Thomas Watson. The two men spent months in a small, noisy workshop, building strange machines and testing them late into the night. On the tenth of March, 1876, something extraordinary happened. Bell was in one room and Watson was in another when Bell spilled some acid on his clothes. He called out, "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you." Watson heard every word through the machine and ran to tell him the good news.

Bell had already received his patent for the telephone a few days earlier, and within a year the new invention was being used in offices and homes. Later he helped to start a company that eventually became one of the largest telephone businesses in the world. Yet he never stopped being a teacher at heart. He spent his later years working on flying machines, boats and medical devices, and he always said that his real success was helping deaf people. When he died in 1922, telephone companies across North America stopped service for one minute to honour him.

Because the doctors worried about his health
Because he wanted to study at a university

items.prompt: When did the families decide to hold the ceremony?
items.passage:
My cousin Dilnoza got married last month, and I want to tell you about the celebration because it was the most colourful wedding I have ever attended. The preparations had started almost half a year before the event. Both families had met several times to discuss the date, the guests and the food. In the end they decided to hold the ceremony in late September, when the weather in Samarkand is warm but not too hot and the fruit in the gardens is ripe.

The celebration began on Thursday evening with a small party called the kina kechasi, or henna night. The women of the family gathered at the bride's house and sang old songs while the bride's friends painted her hands with henna. Dilnoza wore a simple red dress, and my grandmother, who had brought the same songs from her own village, cried a little because she remembered her own wedding fifty years earlier.

On Saturday the main ceremony took place in a big hall decorated with hundreds of white and pink flowers. About four hundred guests had been invited, and many of them had travelled from other cities. The groom, Sardor, arrived in a black car with his brothers and friends, and a band played traditional music at the entrance. The imam read a blessing, and the couple promised to care for each other. Afterwards the bride bowed politely to every older relative, which is a sign of respect that has been kept for centuries.

The dinner was served at eight o'clock. There was plov cooked in huge pots, fresh salads, grilled meat and, of course, tables full of sweets and fruit. Between the courses, relatives performed dances, and even my little brother joined in, although he had said he would be too shy. The party finished after midnight. All the guests agreed that the evening had been unforgettable, warm and full of laughter. Dilnoza says that if she could do it again, she would change nothing, except perhaps the shoes, which hurt her feet by the end of the night.

items.prompt: Where did Aziza grow up?
items.answer: In a small town in the Fergana Valley
items.passage:
When Aziza started her first year at the Tashkent University of Economics, she was both excited and nervous. She had grown up in a small town in the Fergana Valley, and she had never lived away from her parents before. On her first morning she got lost twice on her way to the main building, and she arrived at her lecture ten minutes late. Fortunately, the professor was kind and simply asked her to sit down near the front.

In the beginning, the most difficult thing was managing her time. At school, the teachers had told her exactly what to study every day, but at university she had to organise her own work. She often stayed up until two o'clock in the morning to finish essays, and then she felt too tired to concentrate during classes. After the first exams, in which she received lower marks than she had expected, she decided to change her habits. She bought a notebook, wrote a weekly plan and promised herself to go to bed before midnight.

The change worked. Within a month she was getting better results, and she also had enough free time to join the university debate club. There she met students from many different faculties, and she discovered that she enjoyed speaking in public. Her new friend Kamran, who studied law, taught her how to prepare strong arguments. If she had not joined the club, she says, she would probably still be shy.

Life in the dormitory was not always comfortable. Four girls shared a small room, and the kitchen was often crowded. However, the girls cooked together at weekends, shared notes before exams and helped each other when someone was ill. Aziza now thinks that these friendships are the most valuable part of her education. She is in her third year, and she hopes to work for an international bank after graduation. Her advice to new students is simple: do not be afraid to ask for help, and start preparing for exams earlier than you think you need to.
options: In a small town in the Fergana Valley

title: O'qish 27
intro: Har bir matnni diqqat bilan o'qing va uning savollariga javob bering.

items.prompt: Who used to stop at the bazaar long ago?
items.passage:
Every city has a place where its heart can be felt, and in my hometown that place is the old bazaar. It was founded more than three hundred years ago, when caravans from China and Persia used to stop here to rest and sell their goods. Although the city has changed a great deal since then, the market still stands in the same spot, and many of the shops have been run by the same families for generations.

My uncle Rustam sells dried fruit and nuts at a small stall near the main gate. He starts work at five o'clock in the morning, long before the first customers arrive, because he likes to arrange the apricots, raisins and almonds in neat pyramids. His father had the same stall before him, and he still uses the old brass scales that his grandfather bought in 1950. When I was a child, he let me weigh the nuts for customers, and I felt very important.

The bazaar is divided into sections. In one corner, bakers sell warm bread that has just come out of clay ovens, and the smell reaches you from fifty metres away. In another, coppersmiths hit metal with small hammers, making teapots and trays with beautiful patterns. There is also a covered hall where women sell colourful silk scarves, and a quiet street for spices, where the air smells of pepper, cumin and saffron.

In recent years, the bazaar has had to face new challenges. Big supermarkets have opened nearby, and some young people prefer to shop there because the prices are fixed and there is air conditioning. items.prompt: When is Navruz celebrated?
items.passage:
Navruz is the most joyful holiday of the year in Central Asia. It is celebrated on the twenty-first of March, the day when winter finally gives way to spring, and its history goes back more than three thousand years. The word itself means "new day", and for many families it is the real beginning of the year, with new hopes and new plans.

Preparations usually begin several weeks earlier. Housewives clean their homes from top to bottom, because it is believed that the new year should start in a tidy house. People also pay back old debts and forgive old arguments. In the last week of winter, women prepare sumalak, a sweet dish made from wheat sprouts, flour and water. It must be cooked slowly for about twenty-four hours, and neighbours often take turns stirring the huge pot through the night. They sing songs and tell stories to stay awake, and the evening becomes a small party.

On the day of Navruz itself, the streets are full of people in bright clothes. In the parks and squares, there are concerts, folk dances and sports competitions. Children watch puppet shows, and men try to win wrestling contests, which are among the oldest traditions of the holiday. Many cities organise a large fair where craftsmen sell pottery, carpets and wooden toys. If the weather is good, entire families have picnics under blossoming trees.

The table at Navruz is always generous. Besides sumalak, there are samsa with pumpkin, boiled eggs, nuts and a special soup called halim. Even strangers who happen to pass by are invited inside for a cup of tea. Guests are welcome at any house, and it is considered polite to visit at least three families during the day. Last year, the festival was added to an international list of cultural heritage, and the organisers hope that this will help young people to remember how much the old customs mean. For my grandmother, however, the meaning has never changed: Navruz is simply a day when everybody is kind to everybody else.

items.prompt: Where did Mansur live?
items.passage:
Many centuries ago, a merchant named Mansur lived in Bukhara. He was a quiet man with a sharp mind, and he had made a living by trading silk, spices and paper between Central Asia and the cities of the east. Every spring he gathered a caravan of about forty camels and travelled for nearly six months, crossing deserts and mountains before he reached the markets of China.

The journey was never easy. Before he left, Mansur always studied the weather and the roads, and he hired guides who knew where to find water. Even so, there were dangers. Once, a sandstorm had lasted three days, and the caravan lost two camels and a large part of its food, so the travellers had to wait several days for new supplies to arrive. On another occasion, thieves had followed the travellers for a week, waiting for a chance to attack. Mansur only saved his goods because he had paid a local leader to send soldiers with the caravan.

At the stops along the road, merchants from different countries met, ate together and exchanged news. Mansur learned to speak four languages, and he said that this was more valuable than gold. He also brought back ideas as well as goods. From one trip he returned with the secret of making fine paper, and from another with seeds of new fruit trees that later grew in the gardens of his home city.

When he grew old, Mansur stopped travelling and opened a small guesthouse near the city gate, where he welcomed other caravans. In the evenings, young traders sat around him and listened to his stories. He always ended with the same advice: a successful merchant must be honest, because a damaged reputation travels faster than any camel. Historians say that men like Mansur did more than sell goods. They connected distant peoples and helped science, art and religion to spread across continents, and their influence can still be seen in the cities of the Silk Road today.

items.prompt: How many people live in the narrator's house?
items.passage:
In our house in Namangan, eleven people live under one roof: my grandparents, my parents, my two aunts, my older brother, my sister, my little cousin and me. Many of my friends find this surprising, but for us it is completely normal. In Uzbekistan, it is traditional for several generations to live together, and I have come to believe that this way of life has more advantages than disadvantages.

Of course, there are some difficulties. In the morning, everybody wants to use the bathroom at the same time, so my father made a timetable and stuck it on the door. My sister and I have to share a room, and she often complains that I leave my books on her bed. Dinner is usually noisy because everybody speaks at once, and my grandmother has to ask for silence before we start eating.

On the other hand, we never feel lonely. When I come home from school, there is always somebody who wants to hear about my day. If I have a problem with my homework, my aunt, who is a maths teacher, helps me, and my brother, who studies computer science, explains difficult tasks on the computer. When my mother was ill last winter, the whole family took care of her, and the house never stopped running smoothly.

My grandfather is the head of the family, and everybody respects his opinion. Every Friday he gathers us in the garden and tells stories about his youth. He grew up in a village without electricity, and he walked six kilometres to school every day. We always laugh when he says that today's children would not survive such a walk. He says it kindly, and we all know he is proud of us. Still, I think his stories teach us more than any textbook.

If I move to another city after school, I will probably miss this noisy house very much. Perhaps one day I will have a big family of my own, and I will make a timetable for the bathroom too.

items.prompt: How long have people lived on the site of Samarkand?
items.passage:
Samarkand is one of the oldest cities in the world. Archaeologists believe that people have lived on this site for more than twenty-five centuries, and in ancient times the city was already famous under the name Marakanda. When Alexander the Great arrived in 329 BC, he is said to have described it as even more beautiful than he had imagined.

The city grew rich because it stood at the crossroads of the Silk Road. Merchants brought silk from China, glass from the Mediterranean and horses from the steppes, and Samarkand became a centre of crafts, science and trade. In the thirteenth century, however, it was almost completely destroyed by Mongol armies, and for many years the population was very small.

The greatest period in its history began in 1370, when Amir Timur chose Samarkand as the capital of his empire. He brought skilled builders, painters and scholars from all the countries he had conquered, and he ordered them to create a city that would impress the whole world. During his reign, the huge mosque of Bibi-Khanym and the beautiful Shah-i-Zinda complex were built, with their blue tiles that still shine in the sun today.

His grandson Ulugh Beg continued the tradition of learning. He was a ruler, but he was even more interested in mathematics and astronomy. In the 1420s he built an enormous observatory, where he and his colleagues observed the stars with great accuracy. The catalogue of stars they produced was used by scientists in Europe for more than two hundred years. Sadly, Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449, and the observatory was later destroyed.

Today, visitors come from all over the world to see the Registan Square, where three magnificent madrasas face each other. In 2001, UNESCO added Samarkand to its World Heritage List, and the government has spent a lot of money on repairing the old buildings. Many local people work as guides, ceramic makers or hotel managers, and they are proud that their ancestors left such a remarkable legacy.

items.prompt: Why did the narrator first start going to the library?
items.answer: It was too noisy at home
items.passage:
The central library of our city is a large grey building with tall windows, and I have been going there almost every Saturday since I was twelve. At the time I only wanted a quiet place to read, because my little brothers made so much noise at home that I could not even finish a page. I never imagined that the library would become such an important part of my life.

The building is open from nine o'clock in the morning until eight in the evening, and by half past nine the reading rooms are usually full. Students prepare for exams, retired men read newspapers and young mothers bring small children to the story hour, which is held every Saturday at eleven. The librarian, Mrs Karimova, has worked there for thirty years, and she knows the name of nearly every regular visitor. She always seems to remember what kind of books people like, and she once recommended a novel to me that I still consider my favourite.

In recent years the library has changed a lot. Ten years ago it only had paper books, but now there are also computers, free internet and a section where visitors can borrow e-readers. Some people worried that nobody would visit any more because everything can be found online. In fact, the opposite happened. The number of visitors has increased by almost forty per cent, because the library started organising language clubs, film evenings and workshops for children.

Last month I joined a volunteer programme. Two afternoons a week, I help elderly people to use smartphones and to send messages to their grandchildren abroad. One old gentleman, Mr Usmanov, was so happy when he made his first video call that he brought me a bag of apples the next day. I realised then that a library is not just a collection of books; it is a place where a city shares knowledge and kindness. If I become a teacher one day, I would like to work in a place like this.

items.prompt: Why did the narrator's grandmother move in?
items.passage:
When I was nine years old, my grandmother, Zulfiya, moved in with us after my grandfather died. At first I was not very happy about it, because I had to give her my bedroom and sleep on a folding bed in the living room. However, I soon discovered that she was the best storyteller I had ever met, and I changed my mind completely.

Every evening, after dinner, she sat in her armchair with a cup of green tea and began to talk about her childhood. She was born in 1941, during a difficult time, and her family lived in a small village near Andijan. Her father had gone away to the war and never returned, so her mother had to raise five children alone. My grandmother started working in the cotton fields when she was only eleven. She told me that she used to wake up before sunrise, walk two kilometres to the field and come home with blisters on her hands.

Despite those hard times, her stories were never sad. She remembered the songs the women sang while they worked and the way the neighbours shared their bread when somebody had nothing to eat. She said that the war had taught her people one important lesson: if you help others today, someone will help you tomorrow. She also told me about her teacher, who had walked from house to house to persuade parents to send their daughters to school. Thanks to that teacher, my grandmother learned to read, and later she became a nurse.

I am seventeen now, and my grandmother is eighty-three. Last year I decided to write down her stories before I forgot them. I bought a thick notebook and recorded her voice on my phone as well. My teacher liked the project so much that she suggested I should send it to a national competition for young historians. I did not win, but I received a certificate, and my grandmother kept it on her shelf next to her old photographs. She says it is the most precious thing she owns.

items.passage:
Last weekend our class visited the Museum of Applied Arts, and I think it was the most interesting school trip we have had this year. We met our teacher, Mr Ismoilov, at the bus station at nine o'clock, and after a forty-minute ride we arrived at a beautiful building with a garden full of roses. The museum was once the house of a rich diplomat, and it was built at the beginning of the twentieth century.

A guide named Gulnora welcomed us and gave each of us a small audio device. She explained that the museum keeps over five thousand objects, including embroidery, ceramics, jewellery and wooden furniture from every region of the country. We began with the textile hall, where she showed us a famous silk wall hanging called suzani. items.prompt: Why did the family move to Tashkent?
items.answer: The father got a job and the children could study better
items.passage:
Three years ago, my family moved from a quiet village near Karshi to Tashkent. My father had been offered a job in a construction company, and my parents decided that the capital would give me and my sister better opportunities for education. I was fourteen at the time, and I was not at all happy. I had to leave my friends, my school and my grandfather's orchard, where I had spent every summer of my life.

The first weeks were hard. The city seemed enormous and noisy, with cars everywhere and thousands of people rushing in all directions. I was afraid of the metro, and I took the wrong train on my first day and ended up at the other end of the line. A kind old woman noticed that I looked lost, and she explained how to get back. That small act of kindness made me feel a little better.

School was another challenge. My new class had thirty-two students, and most of them had known each other since the first grade. They spoke quickly, used words I had never heard and often joked about things I did not understand. I sat alone at lunch for nearly a month. Then one day a boy named Timur asked if I wanted to join the school football team. I was not a great player, but I ran fast and worked hard, and soon I had a whole group of friends.

Now I cannot imagine living anywhere else. I love the long boulevards, the tall glass buildings and the evenings when the whole city lights up. There are many things to do: I can visit museums, go to concerts or simply walk by the river with my friends. Of course, I still miss the fresh air and the silence of the village. Every holiday we travel back to see my grandfather, and I help him pick apples. I have learned that you do not have to choose between two places; you can belong to both.

items.prompt: Who usually copied books before the fifteenth century?
items.passage:
Before the fifteenth century, books were extremely rare and expensive. Every copy had to be written by hand, usually by monks who spent months on a single volume. Because of this, only kings, churches and very rich families could afford to own a library, and most ordinary people never saw a book in their entire lives.

Around 1440, a German goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg started to experiment with a new method. He already knew how to work with metal, and he realised that it would be possible to make small metal letters that could be arranged in rows, covered with ink and pressed onto paper. After the page was printed, the letters could be taken apart and used again for the next page. The idea sounds simple today, but it took him many years and a lot of borrowed money to make it work.

His most famous achievement was a Bible, which was completed in about 1455. It is said that around one hundred and eighty copies were produced, and each one was a work of art, with beautiful black letters and hand-painted decorations. However, Gutenberg did not become rich. He had borrowed money from a businessman named Johann Fust, and when he could not pay it back on time, Fust took the equipment and started his own printing business. Gutenberg spent his last years in relative poverty.

The new technology spread extremely fast. By the year 1500, printing workshops had opened in more than two hundred European cities, and millions of books had been produced. Prices fell, more people learned to read, and new ideas travelled across borders in a matter of weeks instead of years. Scientists could share their discoveries, and religious reformers could reach thousands of readers. Many historians believe that without the printing press, the Renaissance and the scientific revolution would have happened much more slowly. Today, in the age of the internet, we sometimes forget that the first information revolution began with a few small pieces of metal.

items.prompt: When is the festival held?
items.answer: On the first Saturday of June
items.passage:
Every year, on the first Saturday of June, the people of our neighbourhood close the main street to traffic and hold a festival. It began eleven years ago, when an elderly teacher named Mr Rakhimov suggested that neighbours should get to know each other better. At that time, many people in our street did not even know the names of those living next door, and he thought that a party would be a good way to change this.

Preparations begin about a month before the event. A committee of volunteers meets every Wednesday evening in the yard of the local school to plan the programme. This year they decided to organise a children's painting contest, a cooking competition and a small concert on a stage built from wooden boxes. My mother, who is a nurse, offered to arrange a free health check for older residents, and my father promised to fix the sound system, which had broken the previous year.

On the day of the festival, the street was full of colour. Neighbours put up tables along the pavement and covered them with bright tablecloths. Everybody brought something to share: homemade bread, pickles, cakes and big bowls of fruit. A grandmother from number twelve won the cooking competition with a delicious pumpkin pie, although she claimed that her granddaughter had done most of the work. In the afternoon, a group of teenagers performed a dance they had been practising for weeks, and even the shyest members of the audience clapped.

The most touching moment came in the evening. Mr Rakhimov, who is now eighty-six and uses a walking stick, walked slowly onto the stage and thanked everybody for keeping his idea alive. He said that a city is not made of buildings but of people who care about each other. The crowd stood up and applauded for nearly a minute. As the lights went down, the children were still running between the tables, and the adults were already discussing next year's plans.

items.prompt: At what age do Finnish children start formal school?
items.passage:
Education systems differ enormously from one country to another, and learning about these differences can help us to understand our own schools better. In Finland, for example, children do not start formal school until the age of seven. Before that, they spend their time playing in kindergarten, and the teachers believe that play is the best way to prepare for later study. Finnish students also have less homework than students in many other countries, and there are almost no standardised tests until the end of secondary school.

In Japan, the school year begins in April, when the cherry trees are in blossom. Students are responsible for keeping their school clean: after lunch, they sweep the floors, wipe the desks and even clean the toilets. Teachers hope that this routine will teach respect for shared spaces. Many Japanese children also attend extra classes in the evening, called juku, because competition for places at good universities is very strong.

In South Korea, the pressure is even greater. Some pupils study until ten or eleven o'clock at night, and the government has tried to limit the number of hours that private academies are allowed to stay open. Critics say that the system produces excellent results but leaves young people exhausted and unhappy. As a result, several schools have introduced free afternoons for sports and hobbies.

In some rural areas of Africa and Asia, the situation is completely different. In many villages, there is only one school for several kilometres, and some children walk for two hours each way. Classes can be very large, with sometimes more than seventy pupils in one room and only a few textbooks to share. Non-governmental organisations have been building new classrooms and providing bicycles so that children, especially girls, can reach school safely.

Experts agree that no single system is perfect. The best results, they say, come when students feel curious and supported, whether they study in a modern city or a small village. If young people enjoy learning, they will continue to learn throughout their lives, and that is the real purpose of education.
